title: Welcome to the IMSI Movement Science Course!
text:
The Integrative Movement Sciences Institute (IMSI) is a National Science Foundation (NSF) Biology Integration Institute dedicated to advancing the understanding of muscular control of movement across organizational scales—from molecular to organismal and ecological.
Our team of leading researchers from universities across the United States is creating a free, fully online course designed to share the excitement of movement science. The course is organized into individual modules covering a variety of movement science topics, which can be explored on their own or combined into curated learning pathways. You can browse modules to find those that spark your curiosity, or follow a recommended pathway to dive deeper into a specific area of the field.

title: Series elasticity
text:
Workshop


Presented by: Dr. Manny Azizi


What is in-series elasticity?
In-series elastic elements are structures that store and return mechanical energy when deformed, positioned in series with the muscles that produce force. Such structures appear across virtually the entire animal kingdom — invertebrates exploit resilient protein-based elements in modified exoskeleton structures, while vertebrates rely primarily on tendons and aponeuroses. Aponeuroses are broad, sheet-like connective tissues that allow muscle fibers to attach over a wider area than a long free tendon permits; they are loaded in more complex ways than free tendons but share the same fundamental elastic function.
Vertebrate tendons are composed predominantly of collagen arranged in a hierarchy of structural levels: tropocollagen molecules assemble into fibrils, fibrils bundle into fibers, and fibers organize into fascicles. Many fascicles constitute the whole tendon. Tendons are metabolically quiet tissues — tenocytes and fibroblasts maintain and repair the collagen matrix, but overall metabolic activity is low. This slow turnover has a practical consequence: tendon remodeling lags substantially behind muscle remodeling. Periods of rapid change in muscle properties (strength training, bed rest, injury recovery) can therefore produce temporary mismatches between the mechanical properties of the two tissues in series.



Tendon material properties: from nonlinearity to viscoelasticity
Stretching a tendon and plotting force against deformation reveals a characteristic nonlinear curve. At low strains the tissue is compliant — this toe region arises because collagen fibers sit in a crimped, wavy configuration at resting length. The initial stretch straightens those crimps before the fibers themselves bear substantial load. Beyond the toe region the relationship becomes roughly linear, and the slope — normalized by cross-sectional area and proportional length change — yields the elastic modulus, a size-independent material constant comparable across species and tissue sizes.
Tendons are not ideal elastic springs. When cycled repeatedly through length changes, they return most but not all of the stored energy. The energy lost per cycle is visible as the area enclosed by the loading and unloading curves (the hysteresis loop), and defines the resilience of the material. Resilience is high in locomotor tendons — studies of key energy-storing tendons report resilience values on the order of 90–93%, meaning very little energy is dissipated per cycle (Ker, Dimery, and Alexander, Journal of Zoology, 1986). The consistent energy loss with each cycle nonetheless confirms that tendon is a viscoelastic material rather than a true elastic spring. A second hallmark of viscoelasticity is stress relaxation: force decays when a tendon is stretched and held at constant length. Together, hysteresis and stress relaxation mean that effective tendon stiffness depends on loading rate, and that the full behavior of tendon cannot be captured by a simple spring model.



A framework for tendon function: three modes of operation
A useful conceptual framework maps tendon function onto the categories already applied to muscle function. Muscles can act as motors (producing energy), struts (producing force without net work), or brakes (absorbing energy). Tendons behave differently in each of these contexts, giving rise to three operational modes:

Power conservation — cyclic behaviors where energy from one stride is recycled into the next
Power amplification — explosive behaviors where tendon storage and rapid release boosts peak mechanical power beyond what muscle alone can deliver
Power attenuation — impact behaviors where the tendon buffers high-power inputs before they reach the muscle fibers

Each mode is explored in the sections that follow.



Power conservation during cyclic locomotion
In walking, running, and hopping, tendons allow muscles to minimize the mechanical work they perform. During ground contact, as the limb loads and the relevant joint flexes, mechanical energy from the center of mass transfers into the stretched tendon while the muscle generates force nearly isometrically — acting as a strut rather than a motor. In the second half of ground contact, as the joint extends, the tendon recoils and returns that stored energy to accelerate the body. Because the tendon handles the energy cycling, the muscle does little net mechanical work.
Classic experiments on tammar wallabies made this process unusually clear. In most running animals, metabolic cost increases approximately linearly with speed. In wallabies, once the animals transition from a quadrupedal running gait to a hopping gait, metabolic expenditure becomes largely independent of hopping speed — a finding established in kangaroos by Dawson and Taylor (Nature, 1973) and confirmed in tammar wallabies and red kangaroos by subsequent work (Biewener et al., J Exp Biol, 2004; Kram and Dawson, Comp Biochem Physiol B, 1998). Measurements of muscle force and fascicle length during hopping showed that the gastrocnemius and plantaris muscles generate large forces with very little length change — operating nearly isometrically — while the ankle joint cycles through large angles of flexion and extension (Biewener, Konieczynski, and Baudinette, J Exp Biol, 1998). Length change at the joint is absorbed by the tendon, not the muscle fibers. As hopping speed increases, the amount of elastic energy cycled through the tendon increases while muscle mechanical work stays approximately constant. The constancy of muscle work across a wide speed range directly accounts for the unusual metabolic independence of speed.
This raises a mechanistic question: why is it cheaper for the muscle to operate isometrically? One hypothesis holds that performing mechanical work (shortening against a load) is inherently more costly than generating force isometrically. Experiments measuring heat production from isolated muscles contracting under different conditions — including an isometric condition and a stretch-shorten cycle — found no significant difference in total energy expenditure between these conditions (Holt, Roberts, and Askew, J Exp Biol, 2014). This result supports a cost-of-force interpretation: the metabolic benefit of isometric operation comes not from avoiding mechanical work per se, but from avoiding the reduction in force capacity that accompanies shortening. When a muscle shortens, its instantaneous force capacity declines (the force-velocity relationship); to maintain a required support force, additional muscle volume must be recruited, and it is the recruited volume of muscle bearing load that drives metabolic cost. Tendons that allow muscles to remain near-isometric therefore reduce the total muscle volume that must be active for force support.



Power amplification: latch-mediated spring actuation
Explosive movements — jumping from rest, rapid acceleration, or climbing steep inclines — require large increases in center-of-mass mechanical energy over a short time. Muscles alone are limited in peak power output by the force-velocity trade-off: high forces require slow shortening, and vice versa. In-series elastic elements provide a mechanism to decouple the time over which muscle performs work from the time over which energy is delivered to the body.
A minimal model of this mechanism has four components: a motor (muscle), a spring (tendon), a latch, and a load (the body mass to be accelerated; Ilton and colleagues, Science, 2018). The motor slowly loads energy into the spring while the latch prevents premature movement of the load. When the latch releases, the spring unloads rapidly — over a shorter time than the motor’s contraction — delivering the stored energy at higher peak power than the motor could sustain. The bow-and-arrow is an everyday analog: the arm is the motor, the bow the spring, the fingers the latch, and the arrow the load.
The quality of the latch determines how efficiently stored energy reaches the load. Rapid, complete release is ideal; a slow or leaky latch dissipates energy during the unlatching phase itself. In vertebrate limbs, effective latching arises from joint geometry: at extreme flexion, mechanical advantage is low and the inertia of the body mass resists extension, holding the system loaded while the muscle builds force. As the limb extends and mechanical advantage increases, the effective latch releases. The timing of this release is sensitive to external conditions — for example, a compliant substrate extends contact time and modifies the effective latch, altering the energy delivery profile.
For a given muscle, there is an optimal tendon stiffness that maximizes stored energy. A spring that is too compliant allows the muscle to shorten so far along the force-velocity curve that force capacity falls before much strain energy accumulates. A spring that is too stiff allows too little shortening for meaningful energy storage. The optimal stiffness balances these limits, and comparative data suggest that muscle and tendon properties are co-tuned across species with different locomotor demands.
Importantly, spring actuation and direct muscle actuation are not mutually exclusive. Hybrid biological-computational experiments — in which isolated frog muscle-tendon units drove a simulated jumping model in real time — showed that during takeoff, the tendon is loaded and begins to recoil, but the muscle continues shortening and delivering mechanical power concurrently with tendon recoil. Contributions from tendon recoil and from ongoing muscle shortening were comparable during the unloading phase. This concurrent operation explains why frog jumping performance is sensitive to temperature even though purely elastic behaviors are temperature-insensitive: the temperature-dependent component is the muscle’s continuing power output during the unloading phase, not the tendon’s recoil per se.



Scaling: when do springs help?
The advantage of spring-driven actuation is not uniform across body sizes. Modeling of latch-mediated spring systems with muscle-like motor properties reveals a size-dependent crossover (Ilton et al., Science, 2018). For very small animals, spring-driven systems dramatically outperform direct muscle actuation across multiple performance metrics. As body mass increases, the inertia of the load increases; accelerating a larger mass takes longer regardless of how rapidly the spring recoils. This inertial constraint progressively erodes the power advantage of the spring, and above a transition body size the benefit diminishes substantially. Animals near this transition can potentially exploit both spring and muscle actuation simultaneously, as the frog experiments illustrate — and whether a given animal benefits more from elastic storage or direct muscle actuation depends on body mass, muscle properties, and the specific performance metric of interest.



Power attenuation: the tendon as a mechanical buffer
Landing from a jump, decelerating, or running downhill all require muscles to absorb and dissipate large amounts of mechanical energy rapidly. Eccentric (active lengthening) muscle contractions can accomplish this, but high-velocity or high-power input applied directly to muscle fibers carries injury risk. In-series tendons reduce this risk by acting as mechanical buffers between the environment and the muscle.
Two complementary mechanisms operate during impact loading. First, at the onset of loading, the activated muscle can shorten against the incoming force — even as the whole muscle-tendon unit is being lengthened — because the tendon absorbs the external deformation. This shortening moves the muscle fibers to shorter, safer positions on the force-length curve before any fascicle stretch occurs. Second, when the tendon subsequently reloads the muscle fibers (as stored energy dissipates and force decays), it does so at a lower velocity than the original external perturbation. The high-power input is temporarily stored in the tendon and released onto the muscle in a slower, more controlled manner.
In vivo recordings of turkeys dropped from height illustrate this buffering (Konow, Azizi, and Roberts, Proc R Soc B, 2012). At impact, as the ankle flexes rapidly, ankle extensor fascicles shorten rather than lengthen — energy enters the tendon, not the fibers. During the subsequent force-decay phase, the tendon recoils and stretches the fascicles, but at velocities substantially lower than the impact velocity. The mechanical power delivered to the whole muscle-tendon unit at impact substantially exceeds the power ultimately delivered to the muscle fascicles, demonstrating significant attenuation of the loading rate.
The timing of muscle activation modulates these protective effects. Anticipatory activation before impact — common in bipedal animals during the aerial phase of locomotion — produces more initial shortening, shifting operating lengths to safer positions before the eccentric phase begins. Activating the muscle earlier promotes greater shortening and moves fibers further up the ascending limb of the force-length curve; later activation reduces this protective shift. Experiments varying activation onset by tens of milliseconds relative to stretch onset showed that, while peak loading rates applied to the fascicles were similar across timing conditions, operating length — the position on the force-length curve during the stretch — differed substantially.
The rate at which the tendon reloads the muscle fibers depends on how quickly the muscle deactivates and force drops, allowing the tendon to recoil. Muscles with faster deactivation kinetics therefore experience faster tendon-mediated loading. This is consistent with the observation that fast-twitch fiber types — particularly fast oxidative glycolytic fibers — tend to show greater susceptibility to eccentric muscle damage than slow oxidative fibers under equivalent activation conditions. The proposed mechanism is that faster relaxation kinetics allow the tendon to recoil at a higher rate, imposing faster stretch velocities on the fibers. This remains a mechanistic hypothesis that warrants direct experimental testing.
An underappreciated consequence of in-series compliance is its effect on proprioception. When fascicles shorten while the whole muscle-tendon unit is being stretched, Ia afferents (muscle spindles) receive signals that do not accurately reflect the external mechanics — the muscle is shortening while the joint is flexing. This decoupling raises the possibility that Golgi tendon organ (Ib) signals, which monitor muscle-tendon force rather than length, carry more relevant information about the external mechanical state in systems with substantial in-series compliance. The implication is that in highly compliant tendon systems, reactive stretch-reflex responses are unlikely to govern the initial protective response; anticipatory, feed-forward motor commands are essential for appropriate pre-contact muscle conditioning.

title: Scaling and dimensional analysis
section: Energy fluctuation patterns of walking and running in terrestrial gaits
text:
Energy fluctuation patterns of walking and running in terrestrial gaits
Walking and running gaits exhibit fundamentally different energy fluctuation patterns that can be understood through spring-loaded inverted pendulum models. In walking, the body operates as an inverted pendulum vaulting over a relatively stiff limb, with the leg acting at nearly fixed length during stance (as humans typically lock out the knee). This creates an out-of-phase relationship between gravitational potential energy and kinetic energy: when the foot first contacts the ground, velocity is at maximum, then kinetic energy converts to potential energy as the body reaches peak height at mid-stance, before reaccelerating and converting potential energy back to kinetic energy in the second half of stance. This passive energy exchange between kinetic and potential energies makes walking economical, requiring minimal external mechanical work on the center of mass. In contrast, running is characterized by bouncing motion where the leg acts as a compliant spring. The center of mass height decreases during stance rather than increasing, resulting in both kinetic energy and potential energy decreasing during the first half of stance and increasing during the second half. These in-phase fluctuations of external mechanical energies mean there cannot be an exchange between kinetic and potential energy; instead, energy is stored in elastic springs within the connective tissues (tendons, ligaments, and muscles) during the first half of stance and released during the second half. The spring-loaded inverted pendulum model, which combines both inverted pendulum and mass-spring dynamics, can account for the coupling between these two modes of motion and successfully predict ground reaction force patterns across diverse bipedal species.

title: Scaling and dimensional analysis
section: Principles of scaling with geometric similarity
text:
Principles of scaling with geometric similarity
The principle of isometric scaling (or geometric similarity) reveals fundamental challenges that arise when animals increase in body size while maintaining the same shape. When an object doubles in linear dimensions while preserving shape, its cross-sectional areas increase by the square of the length change (length²), while volume and mass increase by the cube of the length change (length³). This differential scaling creates a critical biomechanical problem: the ratio of cross-sectional area to mass decreases with increasing size (specifically, as one over length). Since strength in musculoskeletal tissues is proportional to cross-sectional area (scaling as length²) while loading is proportional to body mass (scaling as length³), animals that simply scale up geometrically become relatively weaker as they grow larger. This means larger animals experience relatively higher stresses on their tissues unless they compensate through shape changes. One observed compensation is that large animals adopt more upright, straight-legged postures, which align the bones vertically to better support body weight and reduce the muscular effort required to stand upright. This fundamental scaling challenge—that weight scales much faster than strength—has profound implications for how animals of different sizes must be structured and how they move, leading to systematic changes in both anatomy and locomotor function across the size range from the smallest shrews to the largest elephants.

title: Scaling and dimensional analysis
text:
Dynamic similarity hypothesis
The dynamic similarity hypothesis, developed by Alexander and colleagues in the 1970s-80s, proposes that if locomotor function remains constant across animals of different sizes, then size-related differences should disappear once data are normalized to dimensionless values using a standard set of characteristic physical quantities. For legged terrestrial locomotion, the appropriate base quantities are body mass, leg length, and gravity, derived from considering both inverted pendulum dynamics (with characteristic period related to √(L/g)) and mass-spring dynamics (with characteristic frequency related to √(k/m)). According to this hypothesis, all lengths and distances should be normalized by leg length, forces by body weight (mg), time by the characteristic pendular period √(L/g), frequency by √(g/L), and velocity by √(gL). An important dimensionless quantity is Froude number (v²/gL), which represents the ratio of inertial forces to gravitational forces and equals the square of dimensionless velocity; it is physically impossible for legged systems to walk at Froude numbers greater than one because centripetal accelerations would exceed gravitational acceleration. When locomotion data from species spanning vastly different body sizes are normalized using these dimensionless quantities, the dynamic similarity hypothesis predicts that all variation should collapse onto a single relationship. However, as demonstrated in the bird locomotion data, perfect collapse does not occur—while normalization does reduce variation significantly (particularly in stride frequency), systematic differences remain, with larger birds using relatively higher stride frequencies and shorter stride lengths than smaller birds. These deviations from perfect dynamic similarity reveal functionally important differences in how animals of different sizes actually move, such as large birds employing more vertically bouncy gaits while small birds use flatter center of mass trajectories, reflecting different mechanical strategies and constraints across the body size spectrum.

title: Biophysical muscle models
text:
Overview

Why Model Muscles?
When we move, “everything comes from the muscle” — muscles pull our bones and drive our bodies through space. To simulate, study, or predict movement and posture control, researchers need accurate models of how much force a muscle generates given its activation, length, and velocity. Muscle models are used in two main ways: (1) forward simulation of movement, such as modeling a balance response to a perturbation on a moving platform; and (2) inverse estimation of muscle forces from motion capture and EMG measurements, for example using tools like OpenSim.


The Conventional Approach: Hill-Type Models
The Hill-type muscle model is the most widely used approach in biomechanics. In this phenomenological model, muscle force is estimated as the product of three quantities: activation, a force-length curve, and a force-velocity curve. These curves capture the known fact that muscles produce maximum isometric force at an optimal length and that force decreases at higher shortening velocities. However, the Hill-type model does not capture any history-dependent properties — muscle force is simply a function of current activation, length, and velocity, with no way to account for what the muscle was doing beforehand.


History Dependence: A Problem for Hill-Type Models
Real muscles exhibit substantial history dependence across multiple levels. At the fiber level, a single muscle fiber subjected to a conditioning stretch produces different forces during two portions of lengthening that involve the same velocity and length change — because one portion follows a resting state and the other follows prior movement. At the muscle level, data show different force outputs for the same length trajectory depending on what history preceded it. At the movement level, the “knee pendulum test” demonstrates that a leg dropped from the same height oscillates differently depending on whether it was held still or moving beforehand. In each case, the Hill-type model would predict the same force for identical current states, even though actual forces differ.


The Biophysical Approach: Cross-Bridge Models
The biophysical muscle model is built on the molecular mechanism of active force generation. Active force in muscle comes from cross-bridges — molecular bindings between myosin (thick filament) and actin (thin filament) deep inside muscle fibers; passive force comes from other structural elements. In the simplest version of the model, a cross-bridge is treated as a spring that can exist in two states: attached or detached. Within a muscle, many cross-bridges exist at different displacement lengths from their resting state. The model tracks the distribution of bound cross-bridges across those lengths at each time step, computing how many will transition between states using attachment and detachment rate functions. Attachment rate is highest near zero displacement (resting length) and decreases as cross-bridges are pulled further from equilibrium; detachment rate increases with displacement. Total active muscle force is then the sum of spring forces from all bound cross-bridges.


History Dependence as an Emergent Property
A key insight from the cross-bridge framework is that history dependence arises naturally — it is “an emerging property, rather than we explicitly kept track of the history of everything.” At any instant, the distribution of bound cross-bridges reflects the accumulated history of muscle activation and movement. If a muscle arrives at the same length and activation level via two different paths, it carries different cross-bridge distributions and therefore generates different forces — exactly the behavior observed experimentally, and exactly what the Hill-type model cannot reproduce.


Extending the Model: More States and Calcium Activation
The basic two-state (attached/detached) model can be extended by adding additional states. For example, myosin can enter a “super-relaxed” state in which it is not ready to bind to actin. More importantly, the availability of actin binding sites is controlled by calcium: when the nervous system activates a muscle, calcium ions are released into the muscle fiber, enabling actin sites to become available for cross-bridge binding. Calcium concentration is therefore the activation control signal in simulations. Whether to use a two-state, three-state, or higher-order model depends on which phenomena the researcher needs to reproduce.


Comparing Models: When Does the Transient Matter?
An interactive MATLAB GUI — originally developed for a tutorial at the International Society for Biomechanics (ISB) annual meeting — allows direct comparison of cross-bridge model predictions to Hill-type model predictions. Overall, the two approaches produce comparable force estimates at steady state. The critical difference lies in transient behavior, particularly at the onset of lengthening or shortening. For questions about overall force at steady state, the Hill-type model may be sufficient; for questions where transient force development matters, the cross-bridge model may be more appropriate.


Application: Balance Control and Short-Range Stiffness
Dr. Ryu applies the cross-bridge model to study how humans recover balance after postural perturbations. Experimentally, different joints show distinct torque patterns: the hip develops torque rapidly and then decreases, while ankle torque rises more slowly and remains elevated. When a conventional Hill-type model is used to simulate the first 100 milliseconds after a perturbation, it overestimates the initial body movement — an issue that prior work has linked to the absence of short-range stiffness in the model. Dr. Ryu’s approach grounds this stiffness in cross-bridge mechanics, with the hope that stiffness arising from the physiological process will prove more generalizable across perturbation directions and amplitudes than stiffness prescribed by hand. Coupling the cross-bridge model to an inverted pendulum with tendons of varying compliance suggests that joint-specific torque patterns may reflect a gradient in tendon compliance across the lower limb — a hypothesis that preliminary literature values appear to support. The resulting simulation captures most of the key trends seen in human perturbation data across joints.

title: Balance, stability, and agility
text:
Overview

Evaluating Balance Metrics: A Systematic Comparison
Dr. Sawicki opened by reviewing a paper from Steve Collins’ lab at Stanford that used a rigorous experimental design to test how well six commonly used balance metrics actually detect imbalance. The study applied two types of challenges simultaneously: large-scale perturbations using a multi-directional cable system called the “Bump’em” (attached to participants’ trunks during treadmill walking), and steady disruptions to the physiological systems that normally support balance — blocking vision, locking the ankles, and using pneumatic air jets fired at the swing leg to disturb foot placement. Ten subjects completed the protocol. The six metrics tested were: step width, step time, step placement predictability, Lyapunov exponent, margin of stability, and center-of-mass displacement. The key finding was that performance varied substantially across metrics. Foot placement predictability outperformed all other measures globally, while center-of-mass displacement alone performed no better than chance at detecting whether a person was in an unbalanced state.


Step Placement Predictability
Dr. Sawicki described the step placement predictability framework in more detail. The core idea is that at mid-stance, a person’s center-of-mass position and velocity can be used in a simple linear map to predict where the next footfall will land. This strong linear relationship between mid-stance center-of-mass state and subsequent foot placement suggests that a complex, nonlinear locomotion system may use a relatively simple control rule to regulate balance. The fact that this metric also came out on top in the Collins lab’s systematic comparison provides two lines of evidence supporting it as a useful measure of balance control.


Angular Momentum as a Balance Measure
Another measure Dr. Sawicki highlighted is whole-body angular momentum. From a physics standpoint, keeping angular momentum near zero on average prevents a person from pitching forward to the ground; angular momentum represents the combined rotational contributions of all body segments. Ground reaction forces produce moments around the body’s center of mass that continually regulate this quantity. Work by Anne Silverman showed that even during steady walking (without perturbations), populations at higher fall risk differ measurably in how they regulate angular momentum. For example, amputees show larger-amplitude swings in frontal-plane angular momentum compared to non-amputees, with the difference most pronounced at slow walking speeds. This suggests that frontal-plane angular momentum fluctuation during steady gait may serve as a useful marker of balance impairment. Dr. Sawicki noted, however, that studying angular momentum only during steady walking is limited; understanding balance fully requires also examining how angular momentum responds to large-scale perturbations.


Perturbation Experiments and Exoskeleton Assistance
Dr. Sawicki described several perturbation paradigms his lab uses to study balance beyond steady-state walking. One uses the “Karen” system — a treadmill mounted on a Stewart platform — to deliver phase-locked surface perturbations during walking across 96 combinations of magnitude, direction, and gait phase. Whole-body angular momentum is tracked before, during, and after each perturbation to assess how well the person’s system returns to its steady pattern; the recovery process typically spans multiple steps. Another paradigm uses treadmill belt slips timed to either early or late stance, which either inject or remove mechanical energy from the leg. Research led by Paul in Dr. Sawicki’s lab found that after a belt slip, the contralateral knee’s next step appears to be the primary joint compensating for the energy change. A passive hip spring exoskeleton was tested in this paradigm but did not significantly reduce deviations in angular momentum or mechanical energy following the perturbation, possibly because a passive spring cannot modulate mechanical work with optimal timing.
Dr. Sawicki also described a standing balance exoskeleton study conducted in collaboration with Dr. Lena Ting. An ankle exoskeleton was programmed to apply plantar flexion torque faster than the human nervous system’s own response latency in reaction to a backward surface perturbation. Balance was measured using a psychometric curve approach: perturbation size was progressively increased until participants took a protective step, identifying the size at which stepping occurred more than 50% of the time. Only the condition in which the exoskeleton acted faster than the human’s own response improved this threshold. EMG and ultrasound data further showed that in the fast exoskeleton condition, calf muscle stretch was reduced — yet balance still improved. This suggests that the improvement did not rely on enhanced local ankle reflexes but on a global center-of-mass-level strategy in which information from across the body is integrated to coordinate the balance response.


Defining Stability and Agility Through Energy and Limit Cycles
In the final portion of the workshop, Dr. Sawicki proposed a conceptual framework for defining and measuring both stability and agility using a simple model of rhythmic movement. The experimental platform is a motorized ankle dynamometer: participants lie prone on a table, and their plantar flexors perform a cyclical task that feels like vertical bouncing against a gravitational load, even though only the ankle joint is involved. Participants follow a metronome and aim to maintain a target peak ankle angle. The resulting movement can be represented as a limit cycle in a phase portrait (joint angle vs. angular velocity), and the total mechanical energy of the system (kinetic plus gravitational potential) can be calculated at any point on that cycle.
Stability is then defined as the time constant for the system’s energy to return to its nominal limit-cycle energy (E₀) after the motor injects a perturbation. A shorter time constant indicates a more stable system. Agility is defined using the same energy framework but in a different direction: instead of being knocked off the limit cycle by a perturbation, the participant is given a new target (a higher or lower energy level), and agility is quantified by how quickly the system reaches the new target. A shorter transition time, or equivalently a higher average power over the transition, indicates greater agility. Dr. Sawicki emphasized that this approach uses a common energy currency, making it possible to compare the costs and timescales of stabilization, agile transitions, and metabolic efficiency within one framework.

title: The brain and balance
text:
Overview

Why Balance Control Matters
Balance control is foundational to virtually all voluntary movement. Babies must achieve standing before they can walk, and loss of balance ability can cascade into loss of independence, mobility, and quality of life. In adults over 65, falls are a leading cause of morbidity and mortality — consequences that include injury, loss of independence, and a negative spiral in overall health. Balance impairment is a feature of an exceptionally broad range of conditions spanning musculoskeletal, neurological, and psychiatric disorders, precisely because balance depends on the coordinated function of nearly every part of the nervous system: sensory systems, motor systems, and cognitive systems alike. Even medications — particularly those that cause drowsiness in hospitalized older adults — can substantially elevate fall risk.
Because balance is impaired across so many conditions and populations, it is a tractable entry point for studying fundamental principles of motor control. Balance control lends itself to controlled laboratory study in ways that locomotion does not, while sharing the same underlying neural principles — the mechanisms responsible for corrective balance responses during standing have been found to generalize to corrective torques during perturbed walking as well.


Balance as an Automatic Behavior
Balance control is normally automatic, much like breathing. Under ordinary conditions it is governed by subcortical circuits — the spinal cord and brainstem — without requiring conscious attention. This is evident in everyday experience: a young healthy person can walk and send text messages simultaneously, with neither task demanding full conscious attention. However, in more challenging environments, during difficult tasks, or as a consequence of aging or disease, control of balance shifts toward higher cortical circuits where processing is more deliberate and voluntary.
This shift is a natural and healthy form of flexibility. The problem arises when people must rely on cortical control for activities that should remain automatic — leaving fewer cognitive resources for other simultaneous demands. This is the mechanism behind the common clinical observation that people with fall risk slow down when asked to walk and perform a cognitive task at the same time. It also explains why balance and cognitive health are intertwined: as balance consumes more cortical resources, the margin for other mental activity narrows.


The Sensory Foundations of Balance
Maintaining balance requires answering three distinct questions simultaneously: which way is up (postural orientation), am I falling (equilibrium), and what is my body configuration (posture)? No single sensory system answers all three, which means the nervous system must continuously integrate signals from multiple sources.
Vision can detect relative motion between the observer and the environment, and when a reliable visual reference such as a horizon or vertical wall is present, it can help establish which direction is up. However, vision cannot distinguish whether the observer is moving or the environment is moving — a moving visual surround can trigger a balance response even when the body is stationary, because the nervous system interprets the visual motion as self-motion. Vision also provides no direct information about body configuration unless a person is actively looking at their own limbs.
The vestibular system, located in the inner ear, comprises fluid-filled canals oriented in three planes that detect rotational head motion, and otolith organs that detect linear acceleration and the pull of gravity. The otolith organs function similarly to a small stone resting on a bed of hair cells: wherever gravity or acceleration pushes the stone, the underlying cells fire. This system can indicate which way is up, but tilting the head and accelerating sideways produce the same otolith signal — the two are ambiguous. The vestibular system also encodes head motion, not whole-body configuration, so it cannot directly describe limb posture.
Cutaneous receptors in the skin — especially the pressure-sensitive receptors in the soles of the feet — are critical for balance. The distribution of pressure across the foot surface acts as a continuous map of where ground reaction forces are applied, providing information about the direction of body lean. Cooling the feet reduces this sensation and measurably impairs the ability to stand steadily.
Proprioceptors are particularly important for characterizing body configuration. Muscle spindles are modified muscle fibers that act as sensory organs, firing when their parent muscle is stretched. Golgi tendon organs, located at the muscle-tendon junction, respond to tendon tension. Together these receptors give rise to kinesthesia — the sense of where each body segment is relative to the others. Muscle spindles are also the basis of the familiar tendon-tap reflex: striking the patellar tendon stretches the quadriceps, activating muscle spindle afferents that travel to the spinal cord and cause the same muscle to contract reflexively — a simple example of spinal cord feedback control.
Because none of these systems alone can answer all three balance questions, the nervous system must integrate all of them continuously. Research using blindfolded participants on a tilting platform illustrates this integration: at small tilt amplitudes, participants maintain relatively fixed ankle angles and lean with the platform — a proprioceptive strategy for maintaining joint configuration. As tilt amplitude grows, a vestibular strategy takes over and the head remains relatively stable with respect to gravity even as the platform rotates underneath. People with vestibular loss cannot make this transition and passively tilt with the platform regardless of amplitude.
The ability to shift dynamically between sensory inputs — weighting them according to their reliability in the current context — is a hallmark of a healthy nervous system. When one modality is compromised (as in diabetic neuropathy affecting foot sensation), other senses can partially compensate. Sensory conflict between channels — for example, proprioception indicating one tilt while a moving visual scene suggests another — can produce disorientation or motion sickness. A practical remedy for this conflict, such as the advice to look at the horizon when feeling nauseated on a boat, works by providing a reliable gravitational reference that overrides the conflicting indoor signals.


Perceptual Thresholds and Whole-Body Motion Perception
Effective balance correction requires knowing which direction the body is falling before the right muscle response can be selected. Perceptual thresholds for whole-body motion direction can be measured using a psychophysical paradigm: standing participants are perturbed directly backward on a movable platform, allowed to restabilize over approximately five seconds, and then perturbed again at an angular offset from the backward direction. The participant judges whether the two perturbations felt the same or different. The perceptual threshold — the angular difference at which correct discrimination occurs 50% of the time — is estimated from the resulting psychometric curve.
Two properties of this psychometric curve carry distinct information. The threshold (also called acuity) represents the minimum detectable angular difference. The slope of the curve around the threshold represents perceptual sensitivity — how consistently a person distinguishes perturbations once they are beyond that threshold. A steep slope indicates high certainty in perceptual judgments near the boundary; a shallow slope indicates variability and uncertainty even for clearly different angles.
Research findings show thresholds of approximately 9.5 degrees on average in young adults. Thresholds are elevated in older adults and elevated further in people with Parkinson’s disease and stroke; in some stroke patients, thresholds from ongoing research have been observed approaching approximately 50 degrees — meaning a perturbation aimed nearly perpendicular to backward still felt identical to one directly backward.
In people with Parkinson’s disease (but not in healthy older adults), perceptual threshold correlates significantly with clinical balance scores on the Mini Balance Evaluation Systems Test (Mini-BESTest; maximum score 28). This correlation suggests that some balance deficits in Parkinson’s disease may reflect impaired perception of falling direction rather than impaired muscle force generation. Sensory deficits in Parkinson’s disease appear to span multiple modalities, including proprioceptive and visual processing, rather than being limited to a single channel.


Neural Hierarchies: Spinal Cord, Brainstem, and Cortex
Balance responses arise from a hierarchy of neural circuits operating at different time delays and serving different functional roles. Three levels are most relevant.
At the spinal cord level, responses begin at approximately 50 ms after a perturbation onset. This circuitry drives joint-level co-contraction and stretch reflexes that stiffen joints and maintain local positions. Because spinal circuits operate primarily on proprioceptive signals from individual joints, this level functions more as a postural controller — maintaining body configuration — than as a true balance controller that responds to the direction of whole-body falling.
At the brainstem level, responses occur at approximately 100 ms. Brainstem circuits integrate a broader set of sensory signals and can compute the direction of whole-body motion, enabling coordinated muscle activity across multiple joints simultaneously. Rather than responding to stretch at one joint, brainstem-level control selects the muscle strategy appropriate for the actual falling direction. These circuits are shared between standing balance and walking — the center-of-mass control principles demonstrated in standing perturbation research generalize to corrective torques during perturbed gait, which is why standing balance is a tractable model for studying locomotor control.
At the cortical level, responses arrive later still and reflect higher-order assessment: Is the current strategy working? Should a different strategy be adopted — a step, a grab for support, a change of stance? Cortical involvement signals a shift from automatic to deliberate control and is associated with the kind of flexibility needed when environments change in unexpected ways.
A clarifying example illustrates why brainstem-level control matters. When a platform translates backward, the calf muscle is stretched and a stretch reflex activates it — a correct response for resisting forward sway. However, if the platform tilts forward (rotating the body backward), continuing to activate the calf would worsen the backward fall. Instead, the brainstem-level circuit reverses the command: the calf shuts off and the tibialis anterior activates. This switch requires information about whole-body falling direction, which is why it occurs at the brainstem time scale and cannot be accomplished by spinal proprioceptive reflexes alone.
Co-contraction — simultaneous activation of opposing muscles around a joint — is a postural strategy, not a balance strategy. It can stabilize joints against small perturbations but fails when a large tilt reverses the mechanical demand. Older adults show more co-contraction than younger adults; expert dancers show less. When expert ballet dancers are compared with novices on beam-walking tasks, dancers use the same muscle coordination patterns (synergies) for reactive balance, beam-walking, and overground walking — a pattern consistent with brainstem-level automatic organization even during a challenging task. Novices use more task-specific patterns, consistent with greater cortical engagement. People with better walking ability following stroke similarly show more synergy sharing across tasks, suggesting that automatic brainstem organization is a marker of more recovered motor function.
An important consideration for balance assessment is that faster return to baseline after a perturbation is not necessarily a sign of better balance. A stiffened, co-contracting body may return quickly from small perturbations but is poorly equipped to handle large or directionally varied ones — the perturbations that actually cause falls. A more meaningful measure is robustness: how large a perturbation can a person handle without stepping or falling? Rapid return driven by co-contraction does not translate to robust balance, and can be confounded with truly effective corrective control if speed of return is treated as the primary metric.


Brain Activity During Balance: Beta Oscillations and the N1 Potential
Direct measurement of cortical activity during balance experiments reveals two distinct signals that track individual differences in balance performance.
Pre-perturbation beta oscillations (approximately 13–30 Hz) predict individual differences in perceptual thresholds for whole-body motion direction. Participants with higher beta power in the moments before a perturbation tends to show worse perceptual thresholds. Beta oscillations are thought to reflect a state of reduced sensory receptivity — elevated beta may indicate that the brain is less open to incoming sensory information at that moment. This relationship holds on a trial-by-trial basis: when a burst of beta activity occurs just before a perturbation, discrimination accuracy is lower on that trial. Parkinson’s disease is associated with pathologically elevated beta oscillations in sensorimotor circuits — one of the most replicated findings in movement neuroscience — and this elevated baseline beta may contribute to the impaired whole-body motion perception and balance deficits seen in the disease. People with Parkinson’s also show elevated resting beta during ordinary standing (not just during perceptual tasks), and this elevated resting beta correlates with clinical balance scores.
The N1 potential is a negative voltage deflection of approximately 50 microvolts recorded from the scalp over the supplementary motor area — a region involved in sequential motor planning, located anterior to the primary motor cortex. This amplitude is notably large for a scalp EEG signal. Cortical evoked potentials to balance perturbations have been described in the research literature since the 1980s, and the N1 is interpreted as a balance-error assessment signal reflecting how challenging a perturbation is for that individual.
Several factors modulate N1 amplitude. It is larger when a perturbation is surprising, when a person has fear of falling, or when the perturbation is objectively more severe. It is smaller when the perturbation is anticipated or when attention is divided. In a paired-perturbation paradigm — where a second perturbation follows the first by exactly five seconds — younger adults show a reliably smaller N1 for the second, temporally predictable perturbation. Older adults show less modulation between the two responses. Preliminary data from ongoing research in people with Parkinson’s disease suggests the N1 may remain equally large for both perturbations regardless of predictability, as if each perturbation is equally surprising no matter how many times it has occurred. Over a series of 100 or more perturbations, young adults and older adults show gradual attenuation of the N1 as the stimulus becomes familiar; in some people with Parkinson’s disease or stroke, the response remains flat from the first to the last perturbation — no adaptation at all. This failure to modulate based on temporal context or repetition is another expression of the neural inflexibility that characterizes Parkinson’s disease more broadly.
In young adults, a larger N1 amplitude during a routine standing perturbation predicts worse performance on a beam-walking task — a task that requires the same balance system under greater mechanical challenge. In older adults, a larger N1 correlates with lower balance confidence by self-report and with slower cognitive set-shifting performance on the Trail Making Test. Because it quantifies the subjective challenge posed by the same objective perturbation to different individuals, the N1 may provide a principled way to identify the appropriate training difficulty for each person — calibrating challenge so it is neither too easy (no learning) nor too hard (failure and risk of injury).
The N1 shows good test-retest reliability across sessions separated by one week, and in some individuals by up to one year — a prerequisite for any useful clinical biomarker. This reliability opens the possibility of tracking whether balance health is changing over time, whether a rehabilitation intervention is shifting the neural challenge index in the intended direction, and whether early changes in balance-related brain activity precede detectable deficits on standard clinical tests.


Cognitive Set Shifting and Motor Inflexibility
Executive functions — higher cognitive processes governing attention, planning, and flexible responding — interact meaningfully with motor control for balance. Cognitive set shifting, specifically the ability to update behavioral strategy when the rules of a situation change, is one such function, and impairment in it is associated with fall risk in older adults and people with Parkinson’s disease.
Set shifting is measured clinically using the Trail Making Test. In Part A, participants connect numbered dots in ascending order, assessing basic attention and motor speed. In Part B, they alternate between numbers and letters (1–A–2–B–3–C…), requiring continuous switching between two response rules. Because both parts involve the same number of targets, the additional time needed for Part B beyond Part A is attributed specifically to the cognitive cost of rule-switching. The trail-making test is easily administered with pen and paper in a few minutes, making it practical for clinical and research settings. In older adult and clinical populations, it reliably captures meaningful variation in set-shifting ability. For healthy young adults, however, the task may not be sufficiently challenging to reveal performance differences, and computerized versions with adaptive difficulty or faster stimulus timing may be more sensitive in that population.
The relevance of cognitive set shifting to balance lies in its motor counterpart: motor set shifting is the ability to update muscle coordination patterns when the biomechanical context changes. Research by Fay Horak and colleagues demonstrated this directly. When people stand on a platform and are perturbed backward, a characteristic posterior muscle chain response is elicited. If they are immediately seated and perturbed again in the same direction, healthy individuals rapidly update their responses — lower-limb muscle activity is attenuated and trunk muscles appropriate for seated balance activate instead. People with Parkinson’s disease, however, maintain the lower-limb muscle timing appropriate for standing even in the seated condition, activating muscles that contribute nothing to seated balance correction. Their motor system fails to update its strategy for the changed postural context. This is the motor parallel of the Trail Making Test deficit: just as their cognition fails to switch rules, their motor system fails to switch coordination strategies.
The direction of this motor set-shifting failure also helps explain why it is observed experimentally: participants are moved from the more demanding context (standing) to the less demanding one (seated). In this direction, there is no immediate negative consequence of maintaining the standing muscle pattern — it does not actively impair seated balance, so no error feedback prompts correction. Going from seated to standing would likely produce faster adjustment because the motor system would receive clear negative feedback if it persisted in using a pattern inappropriate for the new demands.
In older adults with no overt clinical deficits, impaired cognitive set shifting (slower Trail Making Test B) correlates with greater muscle co-contraction during balance perturbations. This co-contraction results in smaller center-of-mass displacement after a perturbation — which may appear superficially like better balance — but is the hallmark of a postural stiffening strategy rather than directed corrective control. In these same individuals, the tibialis anterior muscle is inappropriately activated following backward perturbations at a cortical time window — delayed beyond when brainstem-level inhibition should have been sufficient. This suggests that these individuals are not simply relying on a different motor strategy by choice; they appear unable to distinguish forward from backward perturbation direction with enough confidence to appropriately gate the tibialis anterior response.
The overall picture is of a nervous system that cannot efficiently switch its strategy based on context — and this motor inflexibility appears to share underlying mechanisms with cognitive inflexibility as measured on standardized tests. Because balance control in aging increasingly relies on cortical resources shared with executive function, balance assessment should not be limited to purely motor measures. Cognitive assessments, particularly those probing set shifting, provide complementary information that may predict fall risk above and beyond what motor tests reveal.

title: Ultrasound imaging
text:
Overview

Why Measuring Muscle Fascicle Length and Velocity Matters
Knowing the instantaneous length and velocity of a muscle relative to its optimum provides an estimate of that muscle’s current force-generating capacity. The force-length relationship of skeletal muscle follows a characteristic curve with an ascending limb, a plateau at which maximum active force is produced, and a descending limb. Separately, the force-velocity relationship is sigmoidal: positive velocities correspond to muscle shortening and negative velocities to lengthening, with force output changing accordingly. By measuring how fascicle length and velocity shift during real movement, researchers can infer how a muscle’s operating capacity changes from moment to moment — information that is relevant for understanding both why people move the way they do and how movement might be supported or improved.
Workshop-presented research illustrated these principles concretely. Work by Rubensen and colleagues (as presented in this workshop) combined a dynamometer with ultrasound over the soleus muscle to build force-length profiles for individual participants by setting the ankle at different joint angles and measuring maximal voluntary force. When participants then walked with the same ultrasound probe in place, soleus was found to operate around the ascending portion of the force-length plateau — a region that may balance force production with the capacity to resist perturbations or injury-inducing rapid stretch. A separate line of research (presented without confirmed author attribution) showed that the preferred speed at which people choose to transition from walking to running keeps the soleus operating near its optimal fascicle length and at shorter shortening velocities, both of which favor force production. Notably, remaining in a walking gait past this preferred transition speed would cause the energetic cost of walking to exceed that of running. Dr. Jessup’s own group has also demonstrated tight relationships between metabolic cost and fascicle shortening and shortening velocity of calf and quadriceps muscles across different hopping conditions.


How Ultrasound Works
An ultrasound transducer sends high-frequency acoustic waves into the body. When those waves encounter a structure, they reflect back to the transducer, and the computer software converts the speed and strength of those returning echoes into a two-dimensional image. The key property that governs how a structure appears is its echogenicity — that is, how strongly it reflects ultrasonic waves relative to the surrounding tissue. Blood and other fluids are anechoic: they do not reflect ultrasound waves and therefore appear dark in the image, making blood vessels straightforwardly identifiable as dark circles or tubes. By contrast, bone, connective tissue within muscle, tendon, and nerves are echogenic and appear bright white. The outer surface of bone reflects so strongly that ultrasound waves cannot penetrate further, producing a bright white line with a shadow beneath it. Musculoskeletal imaging is performed in B-mode (brightness mode); a separate setting called Doppler mode is used when measuring blood-flow velocity.


Identifying Tissue Structures in Ultrasound Images
Distinguishing between structures in an ultrasound image requires practice and hands-on experience, but some general rules of appearance are useful starting points. Muscle is usually straightforward to identify because of characteristic striations created by interspersed connective tissue and aponeuroses surrounding the muscle belly. Tendon appears circular in cross-section, changes in diameter along its length, and can be traced from the muscle toward its insertion or origin. Nerves are also circular but, unlike tendons, maintain a consistent diameter along their length. Nerves typically run adjacent to blood vessels, and the clinical mnemonic VAN (vein-artery-nerve) can help identify them: the presence of a pulsing anechoic vessel alongside a brighter circular structure is a useful cue. Holding the probe transversely across a limb is generally best for differentiating between structures, while a longitudinal orientation is preferred when the goal is to visualize and track fascicles.


Ultrasound Probe Setup and Integration with Motion Capture
Standard handheld clinical probes cannot be used for measuring fascicle dynamics during movement because they cannot be fixed to the skin while a participant walks, runs, or jumps. Instead, flat-form-factor probes — originally developed for veterinary use and now widely adopted in musculoskeletal biomechanics — can be strapped directly to the limb. Dr. Jessup described placing a foam block of roughly the same dimensions as the probe alongside it within the strapping; the additional surface area this creates helps prevent the probe from rotating or shifting during movement. Cohesive bandage (Co-band) is used to secure the assembly, with the strap tension balanced between probe stability and avoiding excessive deformation of the underlying muscle.
To synchronize ultrasound data with motion capture and force data, the ultrasound module is connected to the broader data-acquisition chain via an analog signal box. A trigger signal — sent simultaneously to both the motion capture system and the ultrasound module — ensures that recording starts and stops at the same time across devices. A return signal from the ultrasound module back to the analog box can serve as a frame-timing check to help realign data if synchronization is disrupted. When using Echo Wave software, a dedicated sync plug-in must be enabled for the system to register external start/stop trigger signals correctly.


Fascicle Tracking Software: UltraTimTrack and UlTrack
Two software tools implemented in MATLAB were demonstrated in this workshop for automated fascicle tracking. The first, UltraTimTrack (developed by Dr. Tim Vanderzee), fuses two computer-vision methods: optical flow and line detection. Optical flow tracks the motion of key pixels or points between consecutive video frames and handles image noise well but is prone to accumulating drift over time. Line detection operates on each frame independently, identifying line-like structures (the fascicles), and is robust to drift but sensitive to noisy images. By combining both methods — with a tunable weighting parameter — UltraTimTrack achieves a balance between noise tolerance and drift resistance, and it performs particularly well for dynamic, high-movement conditions. A sensitivity analysis function within the software allows users to evaluate how the weighting parameter affects the resulting fascicle-length trace.
The second tool, UlTrack (v5.3), uses optical flow alone and is better suited to slow, controlled movements such as passive joint rotations in a dynamometer or a sit-to-stand task. Because it lacks the line-detection component, it is more vulnerable to drift in highly dynamic trials; however, the software includes a keyframe-correction feature that allows the user to anchor fascicle length at defined, repeatable points in the movement cycle and interpolate between them to remove accumulated drift. Both tools allow the user to define the region of interest (the region between the deep and superficial aponeuroses) and to set or import a fascicle manually. The Simple Muscle Architecture plug-in for ImageJ, developed by Neil Cronin, can be used to detect fascicles automatically, with the resulting coordinates imported into UlTrack to remove subjectivity from fascicle selection.


Recommended Acquisition Settings and Limitations
A frame rate of approximately 150 Hz is recommended as a practical trade-off between temporal resolution and image quality, with the maximum achievable frame rate on the systems discussed in this workshop being approximately 210–220 frames per second. Below approximately 100–120 Hz, automated tracking methods show markedly increased noise and inconsistency. Higher frame rates are obtained at the cost of image quality and can require reducing the depth and width of the field of view; settings that most strongly affect frame rate include image depth, image width, and the number of ultrasonic beams used per scan. A field of view of approximately 50 mm depth by 40 mm width was used in the examples shown.


Advantages, Limitations, and Q&A Discussion
Relative to sonomicrometry — a technique in which two sensors are surgically implanted along the length of a fascicle, currently used only in animal research — ultrasound’s main advantages are that it is non-invasive, provides contextual information about the motion of surrounding structures, and is portable and relatively straightforward to synchronize with other data-acquisition systems. Its principal limitations are a relatively low maximum temporal resolution (approximately 200 Hz at full image quality sacrifice) and the reliance on computer-vision algorithms that are imperfect, particularly for very fast or highly perturbed movements.
In the Q&A discussion, workshop participants raised several practical topics. Dr. Kiisa Nishikawa asked about limitations for highly dynamic movement research; Dr. Jessup indicated that the main constraint is frame rate, but that current tracking algorithms are capable enough that even perturbed-movement studies appear feasible. Jill McNitt-Gray raised the possibility of integrating portable ultrasound into field settings such as a pop-up motion-capture arena, noting the potential for combining muscle-level and whole-body kinematic data. Dr. Monica Daley observed that wireless transmission of ultrasound data would involve significant bandwidth trade-offs relative to wired systems, given how data-intensive ultrasound video is. Participants also discussed the value of universal timestamping as a strategy for synchronizing ultrasound with independently recorded video in non-laboratory settings.

title: Data visualization and statistical inference for biomechanics
text:
Overview

Research goals and sources of variability
Dr. Finley opened by framing the workshop around a central question posed to participants: what is the primary goal of scientists? Responses converged on themes of answering questions, generating knowledge, and understanding the world. He then outlined four broad categories of research: descriptive studies that characterize populations; methods-development studies focused on the validity and reliability of measurement tools; studies of relationships between variables using tools such as correlation and regression; and experimental studies aimed at establishing cause-and-effect relationships.
A recurring theme was variability. Finley identified three types relevant to research design. Concomitant variation — the change in a dependent variable when the independent variable is manipulated — is the variability that enables causal inference. Extraneous variability, introduced by inconsistent measurement across sessions, imprecise or inaccurate instruments, or uncontrolled participant characteristics such as fluctuating alertness, reduces the ability to detect true effects. Confounding variables constitute a third source that can prevent researchers from establishing causality altogether. He described statistics as tools for both quantifying and explaining these sources of variability.


Anscombe’s Quartet: the limits of summary statistics
To illustrate the dangers of relying on summary statistics alone, Finley walked participants through Anscombe’s Quartet — four data sets that are visually very different but share nearly identical statistical properties. Using a MATLAB script provided in a shared Google Drive folder, participants computed the mean and standard deviation of each data set’s X and Y values, then fit a linear regression to each, obtaining slope, intercept, and R-squared values. In every case, the values were essentially identical across all four data sets. Yet when the data are plotted, it is immediately clear that a linear model is only appropriate for the first data set; the others show curvature, outliers, or degenerate structure that makes the fitted line meaningless.
The key take-home from this exercise was stated directly: looking at summary statistics alone — whether descriptive statistics such as mean and standard deviation, or inferential statistics such as R-squared — does not reveal how the underlying data actually look. This problem is especially pronounced with small samples, which are common in biomechanics, human, and animal model research. Finley’s recommendation was to visualize data early and often throughout the entire analysis pipeline, from the moment of data collection through each subsequent processing step.


Making publication-ready figures in MATLAB
Finley presented a workflow for creating figures he described as publication-ready, illustrated using a second MATLAB script applied to the same Anscombe’s Quartet data. A central comparison in this section was between a bar plot with error bars and a dot plot showing individual data points and medians. When displayed as a bar chart, all four Anscombe data sets appeared similar in spread. When displayed as a dot plot, differences in the distribution and the presence of outliers became immediately apparent. This reinforced the earlier point that the choice of visualization method itself can either reveal or conceal the structure of data.
Specific recommendations for figure formatting included: always labeling axes with full words and units; using MATLAB’s set function to control properties such as face color, edge color, line width, and font size in code rather than by post-processing in a separate illustration program; and specifying figure dimensions in centimeters so that the exported file matches the intended print size (for example, one and a half columns in a standard two-column journal format). He recommended saving figures in multiple formats: a MATLAB .fig file for later in-program editing, a PDF for annotation or presentation, and a TIFF for journal submission, noting that TIFF files preserve more image information than JPEG, which uses compression. He also noted that sub-panel labels (A, B, etc.) can be added directly in MATLAB code using the text command, specifying X and Y coordinates for label placement. His general principle was to encode all figure formatting choices in code so that figures can be regenerated automatically when analyses are revised.


Understanding p-values through simulation
The third major section addressed inferential statistics and the meaning of p-values. Finley introduced a simulated experiment designed to make the concept concrete: 1,000 independent studies each tested whether drinking one ounce of water improved long-jump performance in Olympic male athletes. Because the intervention has no plausible effect on jump distance, the null hypothesis was known to be true by construction. In the simulation, each study drew 100 participants from a control population with a mean long-jump distance of 8 meters and a standard deviation of 20 cm, and 100 participants from an identically specified test population, then compared the two groups using a t-test.
Across 1,000 simulations, the resulting p-values followed a roughly uniform distribution between 0 and 1. The false positive rate — the proportion of experiments that returned p < 0.05 despite the null hypothesis being true — was approximately 0.048, close to 0.05. Finley used this demonstration to give concrete meaning to the standard definition: the p-value is the probability of obtaining a result at least as extreme as the observed one if the null hypothesis were true. A p-value does not indicate how important or scientifically meaningful a finding is.
Finley also referenced a 2015 paper titled “Estimating the Reproducibility of Psychological Science,” in which a large group of researchers attempted to replicate findings from prominent psychology journals. In the original published studies, nearly all had p-values below 0.05; in the replications, the median p-value was above 0.2, and only a small percentage of studies replicated at the conventional threshold. He placed this paper in the shared folder for participants to read. During the Q&A portion of the session, Finley noted that p-values are also influenced by sample size: with very large data sets, p < 0.05 is almost always obtained, but this only means that very small effects can be detected — not that those effects are meaningful.


Sample size, statistical power, and effect size
In the final section, Finley introduced the concepts of sample size and statistical power. He explained that MATLAB includes a built-in function for computing required sample size given a specified statistical test, the expected distribution under the null hypothesis, the expected difference between groups (effect size), and the desired power level. As an illustrative example, he described a study comparing vertical jump height between two groups of students, where pilot data showed a mean jump of 50 cm with a standard deviation of 4 cm. To detect a group difference of 2 cm with adequate power, the function returned a required sample size of 34 individuals per group.
Finley described the general relationships between these quantities: higher desired power requires a larger sample; smaller effect sizes also require larger samples to detect. Conversely, when researchers are limited in the participants or observations they can collect, they are best positioned to study effects that are likely to be large. He also drew a distinction between statistical significance and practical importance, noting that “significant” in everyday language implies importance, which is not guaranteed by p < 0.05. Effect sizes and their uncertainty — rather than p-values alone — were described as the more meaningful quantities to report and interpret.
During the Q&A portion, a participant asked how researchers determine what effect size is interesting. Finley noted that in clinical research, practitioners sometimes define a minimally clinically important difference — for example, a 0.4 meters per second change in walking speed, which might allow a person to cross a street before a traffic light changes. He acknowledged that equivalent benchmarks are rarely available in basic science research, and that researchers must make and defend their own judgments about what effect magnitudes matter, considering what a difference would enable functionally. He also mentioned confidence intervals and Bayesian methods as additional tools for characterizing uncertainty in effect estimates beyond the p-value.
