title: Computational modeling
text:
Overview

Introduction to Computational Modeling in Muscle Biology
Computational modeling uses mathematics and computation to study complex biological systems across different organizational scales. In the context of muscle biology, models range from describing simple chemical reactions—such as how two molecular species combine to form a third, captured by a set of differential equations—all the way up to simulating the coordinated mechanics of many interacting filaments within a sarcomere. Dr. Tanner’s lab integrates computational modeling with biophysical experiments (primarily single-fiber mechanics using skinned fibers) to investigate the molecular mechanisms of muscle contraction. The proteins at the center of these models include the thin filaments (primarily actin), the thick filaments (myosin), and regulatory proteins such as troponin, tropomyosin, and myosin binding protein C.


A Brief History: The Hill Model
One of the earliest influential models of muscle force production was developed by A.V. Hill, who shared the 1922 Nobel Prize for linking heat production and mechanical work in muscles. The Hill model represented muscle as three components: a passive element, a contractile element, and a series element (which can be thought of as representing the tendon or other in-series compliance). Together these produced a force-length relationship with recognizable features: the passive component contributes little force at resting length but grows substantially at longer lengths; the active (contractile) component shows an ascending limb, a plateau, and a descending limb; and the total (combined) force reflects a trade-off between these two contributions. Despite its simplicity, this framework has remained widely useful for describing how muscle force changes with length.


Crossbridge Theory: The Huxley 1957 Model
A major conceptual advance came from Andrew Huxley’s 1957 paper, which introduced the idea that myosin crossbridges interact with actin binding sites in a position-dependent manner as the filaments slide past one another. In this model, the rate of crossbridge attachment (called f) and the rate of detachment (called g) both depend on the spatial position or distortion of the crossbridge—that is, how far the myosin head is displaced from its optimal alignment relative to the nearest actin binding site. When filaments are not moving (isometric conditions), a high proportion of crossbridges are bound and substantial force is generated. As shortening velocity increases, the distribution of bound crossbridges shifts and total force decreases, reproducing the well-known force-velocity relationship. A further refinement came from Huxley and Simmons in their 1971 paper, which proposed a crossbridge power stroke: a conformational change in the neck region of the myosin head (visible in structural data as the head moving from one angular position to another) that constitutes the force-generating event.


Spatially Explicit Two-Filament Models
Through much of the history of muscle modeling it was assumed that thick and thin filaments are rigid—that all the compliance in the system comes from the crossbridges themselves. If the filaments do not stretch, then the mechanical state of one actin–myosin pair is identical to every other pair, and a single interaction can represent the whole population. However, X-ray diffraction measurements from the mid-1990s provided evidence that both thick and thin filaments are themselves elastic (extensible). This finding meant that neighboring crossbridges along a filament can be in different mechanical states depending on whether and how their neighbors are bound, making a population-level spatial model necessary.
This motivated the two-filament spatially explicit model published by Daniel and colleagues in 1998. The model represented a half-sarcomere using 20 thick filament nodes (positions from which crossbridges extend) and 30 actin binding sites on the thin filament, with linear elastic springs connecting adjacent nodes along each filament. The different node counts reflect the different periodicities of the two filament types (approximately 43 nm for the thick filament and approximately 37 nm for the thin filament, though the transcript wording was garbled on this point). Because solving large systems of ordinary or partial differential equations for position-dependent crossbridge kinetics is computationally difficult, the model used Monte Carlo (stochastic) algorithms in which crossbridge attachment and detachment are governed by probabilities derived from position-dependent rate functions rather than solved analytically.


Multiple Filament Models and Physiological Geometry
In the physiological sarcomere, the filament arrangement is not a simple one-to-one pairing: each thick filament interacts with six thin filaments, and each thin filament interacts with three thick filaments. Dr. Tanner’s doctoral work extended the two-filament framework to simulate this physiological lattice geometry. To avoid the edge effects that arise in a finite lattice, the model simulated 4 thick filaments and 8 thin filaments but applied periodic boundary conditions—effectively wrapping the edges of the simulated region onto each other to approximate an infinite lattice with a finite number of filaments. The model also incorporated calcium-dependent thin filament activation through a three-state kinetic cycle.
When compared to the two-filament model at the same calcium levels, the multiple-filament model predicted substantially higher force per myosin and greater crossbridge binding. At a high calcium level (pCa 4), the multiple-filament model predicted approximately 2 piconewtons per crossbridge, compared to approximately 0.5 piconewtons for the two-filament model—values that aligned better with data from single-molecule experiments. The key mechanism underlying this difference is compliant realignment: when a crossbridge binds and undergoes its power stroke, it displaces the thin filament relative to the thick filament, bringing neighboring crossbridge heads into more favorable alignment for binding. This cooperative recruitment is amplified as more filaments interact, because each binding event affects a larger mechanical neighborhood.


Extensions to the Spatially Explicit Framework
Several groups have extended these spatially explicit models in different directions. Some models have added titin as a passive spring element connecting the free end of the myosin to the Z disk, showing that titin has a significant effect on passive force as sarcomere length changes. Others have incorporated myosin binding protein C (located in the C zone of the thick filament), which competes with actin binding—reducing crossbridge availability—through a kinetic scheme that represents its stabilizing effect on the myosin head. Additional work has addressed the three-dimensional nature of crossbridge motion, since crossbridges undergo both a longitudinal (along-filament) displacement and a torsional or transverse component during the power stroke, with implications for lattice spacing as muscle length changes. One group has also used spatially explicit frameworks to simulate muscle twitches and work loops, allowing examination of stress, strain, and energy use during dynamic contractions.


Code Demonstration
Dr. Tanner demonstrated a MATLAB implementation of the two-filament Monte Carlo model, written to closely follow the Daniel et al. 1998 framework and made available for download in the workshop research folder. The main script calls a parameter file (where values such as filament spring constants can be modified), a model-building function that establishes node positions and tracks which crossbridge nodes can interact with which actin binding sites, and a kinetics rate function that evaluates position-dependent attachment and detachment probabilities. The model is run multiple times (e.g., 25 repetitions) and forces are averaged across runs to reduce stochastic variability. Outputs include mean force (in piconewtons) and the fraction of crossbridge heads bound, both plotted as a function of time; an exponential fit extracts the asymptotic force level and the rate constant to half-maximum. In a live demonstration, reducing thin filament stiffness to one-tenth of its default value produced slightly less force (because more mechanical energy was absorbed by filament stretching rather than converted to force output) while increasing the fraction of bound crossbridges—illustrating the interplay between filament compliance and force production that motivated this class of models in the first place.


Q&A: Thick Filament Activation, Disease, and Choosing a Model
During the Q&A portion of the workshop, participants raised several topics extending beyond the main presentation. On thick filament activation and the super-relaxed state of myosin: Dr. Tanner described how this could in principle be incorporated by adding a mechanically sensitive transition in the kinetic scheme, where the rate of transition from the super-relaxed state to the disordered-relaxed state (which makes myosin heads available to interact with actin) would depend on the local mechanical strain along the thick filament—the stretch of the spring segments between thick filament nodes. On disease and injury: the discussion noted that molecular-level mutations affecting troponin, tropomyosin, or myosin kinetics (for example, prolonged crossbridge attachment due to impaired detachment) could be simulated by changing kinetic rate functions, while tissue-level changes such as collagen deposition during injury recovery could be incorporated as modified passive mechanical elements, analogous to the parallel passive element in the Hill model. On choosing the right model for a given question: Dr. Tanner emphasized that the model must include a parameter or subsystem representing the process being studied—if there is no “control knob” for the variable of interest, the model cannot answer the question. The key practical challenge is deciding how much to include, since incorporating full spatial detail greatly increases computational cost.

title: So you want to simulate movement?
text:
Overview

Why Simulate Movement?
Dr. Hubicki opened by explaining that simulation connects experimental biology and robotics. In his research, he builds computer simulations of robots to develop controllers for walking machines. He introduced the guinea fowl as an example of an animal studied experimentally by Dr. Monica Daley, noting that experiments are essential for collecting data but that simulations offer a complementary way to interrogate motion. A simulation allows researchers to test hypotheses and explore conditions that would be impossible to apply to a live animal—without requiring further experiments, or in direct complement to them.


Math Models Come in Many Forms
Dr. Hubicki showed that math models of movement can range from highly detailed musculoskeletal models—such as those built in OpenSim (which Dr. Hubicki noted has been downloaded hundreds of thousands of times)—to very simple reduced-order models. He described a 2006 paper by Monica Daley in which a spring-loaded inverted pendulum (SLIP) model was used to study how a guinea fowl maintains stability when stepping into an obstacle. Simple models are also central to robotics: a bio-inspired reduced-order model can, in principle, yield animal-like movement as a consequence of optimizing control within that model.


Dynamical Systems and Differential Equations
To simulate movement, a mathematical model of the system is needed—specifically, a dynamical system: a system whose behavior changes over time and is described by the time derivatives of key variables called state variables. These relationships are expressed as differential equations, which are equations that contain derivatives. Dr. Hubicki used a simple population growth model (dP/dt = αP) as a first example. Its exact analytical solution is the exponential function P(t) = Ce^(αt), where the constant C is set by the initial condition (the starting population). He then introduced the pendulum: its governing differential equation (d²θ/dt² = −(g/L)sin(θ)) cannot be solved exactly using elementary functions such as sines, cosines, or exponentials—a long-established mathematical fact—so a different approach is needed.


Euler’s Method: Numerical Approximation
Because many differential equations cannot be solved analytically, simulation relies on approximate numerical solutions. The simplest such approach is Euler’s method, derived directly from the definition of a derivative: X(t+Δt) ≈ X(t) + (dX/dt)·Δt. By repeatedly applying this update rule with a small time step Δt, the simulation steps forward through time. Dr. Hubicki implemented this in MATLAB with the population growth model, producing an exponential growth curve consistent with the analytical solution. He demonstrated that accuracy depends on the size of the time step: using too large a Δt caused a simulated conservative spring system to spuriously gain energy over time, while reducing Δt substantially corrected the error.


State Variables and Systems of First-Order ODEs
Euler’s method as derived applies only to first-order ordinary differential equations (ODEs)—equations containing a single time derivative. Mechanical systems governed by Newton’s second law (F = ma) typically involve second-order derivatives (acceleration). To handle this, Dr. Hubicki introduced state variables: by defining both position and velocity as separate variables, a second-order equation can be rewritten as two coupled first-order ODEs. The collection of these variables is called the state vector. He emphasized that the state vector must contain exactly the information needed to simulate the system forward in time—for a moving mass, that is its current position and velocity.


Simulating the 1D Spring-Loaded Inverted Pendulum in MATLAB
Dr. Hubicki built a one-dimensional SLIP model in MATLAB from scratch: a point mass on a spring under gravity, with vertical position Z(t) as the single coordinate. The equation of motion, derived by summing forces (gravity downward and spring force upward), is MZ̈ = −Mg + K(L₀ − Z), where M is the mass, g is gravitational acceleration, K is the spring constant, and L₀ is the spring rest length. Defining state variables Z and dZ/dt, he derived two first-order ODEs and applied Euler’s method in a for loop, pre-allocating output arrays before the loop for efficiency. He then introduced MATLAB’s built-in ODE45 solver, which automatically adapts its time step by comparing the results of 4th- and 5th-order Runge-Kutta integration steps, producing more accurate simulations without manual tuning of Δt.


Hybrid Dynamics, Liftoff, and Q&A
To allow the SLIP model to leave the ground and hop, Dr. Hubicki explained that the system becomes a hybrid dynamical system—one whose governing equations switch between different forms depending on the phase of motion (stance versus flight). In the flight phase, only gravity acts on the mass; in stance, the spring force is also active. He implemented this as a simple conditional in MATLAB: when height Z exceeds the spring rest length L₀, the spring force is set to zero. During the Q&A, he explained this switching condition in physical terms—ground contact is unilateral, meaning the ground can only push up and cannot pull the foot down, so once the spring passes its natural length and would need to tug the mass earthward, the foot leaves the ground and flight begins. He also noted that ODE45 includes an event detection feature that can identify the precise moment of liftoff or touchdown, enabling more accurate handling of these phase transitions than a simple conditional check within a fixed-step loop.

title: Using motion capture and electromyography (EMG) in movement sciences
text:
Overview

Inverse Kinematics: Estimating Joint Angles
Inverse kinematics is a technique foundational to all motion capture software. It is used whenever joint angles need to be estimated from limited information — for example, at joint centers with no accessible bony landmark, such as the hip in humans, or at joints in animal models where placing markers directly is not feasible. Markerless motion capture systems use inverse kinematics internally to constrain their pose estimates to anatomically realistic configurations. The technique also applies when filling gaps in marker data: when a reflective marker is occluded during a trial, the software can estimate the missing joint angle from the angles of the remaining visible markers. The workshop worked through a hands-on example using the law of cosines to compute ankle and knee angles in a squatting figure, given known segment lengths and hip height. A key discussion point was that when taking the arc cosine to solve for a joint angle, the solution could be positive or negative; biological constraints typically allow only one of those answers (for example, a negative value would correspond to the knee bending backwards, which is not anatomically plausible in humans).


Inverse Dynamics: Computing Joint Moments
Inverse dynamics extends kinematic data to estimate joint moments by incorporating force information. Two complementary approaches were presented. The bottom-up approach starts from ground reaction forces measured by a force plate beneath the subject’s feet and uses the moment arm — the perpendicular distance from the force’s line of action to the joint center of interest — to compute moments, working upward through the body segment by segment. The top-down approach begins from a location where the external force is known or can be assumed: for example, no external force acts on the head, and a leg in swing phase during walking has no ground contact force. Starting from either of these locations and working toward the body’s center or lower extremities yields joint moment estimates by the same moment-arm logic. OpenSim uses both approaches simultaneously and compares their results; minimizing the difference between bottom-up and top-down estimates serves as an indicator of overall data quality. During Q&A, the group discussed using the right-hand rule (the cross product R × F, where R is the moment arm vector and F is the force vector) to formally determine the sign of a joint moment, and clarified that a free-body diagram can be cut at any joint provided all forces on the isolated segment are fully accounted for.


Best Practices for Motion Capture Data Collection
Motion capture is not a single measurement but a sequential pipeline of processing steps: markers are placed on the subject, cameras emit infrared light and detect the reflections from passive markers, software triangulates three-dimensional marker positions from multiple camera views, those trajectories are used to build a biomechanical model, and biomechanical variables are then computed. Error introduced at any stage accumulates as data moves through the pipeline. Markers are placed on bony landmarks to minimize soft tissue artifact — the displacement of a marker relative to the underlying bone when overlying skin or muscle tissue shifts during movement, which the software incorrectly interprets as bone movement. A single camera can only determine where a marker falls in its two-dimensional image; at least two calibrated cameras are required to triangulate a marker’s three-dimensional position. Markerless systems use computer vision algorithms, typically neural networks, to identify anatomical landmarks directly from video, which is particularly useful for small animals or behaviors where markers would be occluded or would interfere with the movement. A minimum inter-marker distance must be respected because markers placed too close together can switch trajectories between frames. Practical recommendations included using tight-fitting clothing, calibrating the lab system appropriately on each data collection day, monitoring marker trajectories throughout each trial with the help of an assistant, having participants cross their arms when they would otherwise occlude trunk markers, and re-collecting any questionable trial immediately rather than attempting to repair it during processing.


How EMG Works: Bipolar Electrodes and Signal Generation
Electromyography (EMG) captures information about the timing, magnitude, and duration of muscle activation. The signal originates in the spinal cord: alpha motor neuron cell bodies receive excitatory and inhibitory inputs at their dendrites, and when the summed input crosses threshold, an action potential travels along the motor neuron to the neuromuscular junction. At that junction, acetylcholine is released, which changes the membrane permeability of the muscle fiber and triggers a fiber-level action potential through sodium influx and subsequent calcium release, causing muscle contraction. A bipolar electrode detects the voltage difference between two electrode sites as this action potential propagates along the length of the muscle fiber. Surface EMG records the summed activity from many motor units across a volume of muscle, producing the characteristically noisy waveform familiar from published data. For bipolar electrodes to register a meaningful voltage difference, they must be oriented parallel — not perpendicular — to the muscle fiber direction. If the two electrodes are positioned such that they straddle the neuromuscular junction, the action potential reaches both electrodes simultaneously and the voltage difference is zero. In animal models, fine wire electrodes consist of a twisted pair of stainless steel wires that are insulated along their length with bare tips, inserted into the target muscle via a hypodermic needle.


Best Practices for EMG Data Collection
Reliable EMG recordings depend primarily on correct electrode placement. For human subjects, electrode placement begins with anatomical knowledge of the muscle’s origin, insertion, and function. Published electrode placement guidelines (referred to in the workshop as the “CDM guidelines”) provide recommended sensor placement procedures and anatomical reference information organized by muscle; presenters noted that these should be used as a starting point rather than followed rigidly, because the reference models tend to be able-bodied individuals and individual anatomy varies. Palpating for the target muscle while asking the participant to volitionally contract it — pressing firmly rather than lightly — is the most reliable way to confirm where the muscle lies before placing the electrode. Skin preparation (exfoliating with a product such as NuPrep, then wiping with alcohol) reduces impedance between electrode and skin. Electrodes and their associated hardware should be secured to prevent movement artifact, and placement should be verified by checking for clear activation bursts in the recording software before data collection begins. For animal models, the most critical preparatory step is testing the fine wire electrodes with a multimeter before insertion — checking for conductivity and confirming insulation is intact except at the bare tips — because stimulation-based verification of placement is generally not feasible. Keeping wire lengths short, securing wires to nearby tissue after insertion, and pressing down as the needle is withdrawn all reduce noise introduced by wire movement.


EMG Signal Processing: From Raw Signal to Envelope
The standard pipeline for processing surface EMG has three main steps. First, a high-pass filter (typically at approximately 20–30 Hz) is applied to the raw signal to remove the DC offset and any low-frequency motion artifacts. Second, full-wave rectification takes the absolute value of the filtered signal, converting all negative deflections to positive so the signal lies entirely on one side of zero. Third, a low-pass filter (typically at approximately 10–20 Hz) smooths the rectified signal into the EMG envelope — the representation most commonly shown in published literature and used for interpreting muscle activation patterns. Fast Fourier transformation (FFT) is a useful diagnostic tool before filter design: it converts the raw EMG signal from the time domain into the frequency domain, producing a power spectrum that shows which frequencies are present and at what magnitude. Inspecting this spectrum helps identify, for example, a 50 Hz spike from AC electrical sources (lights, power cables) that can be targeted with a notch filter. Butterworth filters are the most common implementation and come in low-pass, high-pass, bandpass, and notch variants; the cutoff frequency and filter order (which controls how sharply the filter attenuates frequencies beyond the cutoff) are the two main design parameters. Signal decomposition is a distinct analytical approach that uses electrode arrays and complex algorithms to separate the raw EMG into individual motor unit action potential trains, providing finer insight into motor control; it requires intramuscular or two-dimensional electrode arrays and is not feasible with standard bipolar surface electrodes. The workshop concluded with a MATLAB live script tutorial that stepped participants through the full processing pipeline using human tibialis anterior EMG data and rat walking data recorded from an animal model of Parkinson’s disease.

title: Modeling the muscle spindle
text:
Overview

Anatomy and function of the muscle spindle
The muscle spindle is a small sensory structure embedded within skeletal muscle and assumed to lie in parallel with the surrounding extrafusal muscle fibers. Inside its capsule are intrafusal muscle fibers, of which there are three types: bag 1, bag 2, and chain. Because bag 2 and chain fibers have similar mechanical properties, this model groups them together, treating the spindle as containing two functional fiber populations — bag and chain.
Two afferent pathways relay spindle signals to the central nervous system. The primary 1A afferent reads from all intrafusal fiber types (both bag and chain) and is the focus of this workshop. The group 2 afferent connects only to chain fibers and also contributes to proprioception, but is not modeled here.
Unlike most sensory organs, the muscle spindle receives its own motor drive, the fusimotor (gamma motor) system. Gamma dynamic motor neurons project to the bag fiber; gamma static motor neurons project to the chain fiber. The larger extrafusal muscle, by contrast, is driven by alpha motor neurons. The 1A afferent monosynaptically synapses onto alpha motor neurons, forming the substrate for the classic tendon tap reflex: tapping the patellar tendon stretches the quadriceps, which stretches the embedded spindle, activating 1A afferents that reflexively contract the muscle.
The 1B afferent, which originates from the Golgi tendon organ at the interface of the extrafusal muscle and tendon, measures extrafusal force during contraction. It is not part of the muscle spindle and is not included in this model.


History dependence of spindle firing
A key feature of 1A afferent firing is that it is history-dependent, paralleling the history dependence already known for extrafusal muscle force output. When a resting spindle is first stretched, it produces an initial burst of high firing rate, analogous to short-range stiffness in extrafusal muscle. A subsequent stretch of the same amplitude does not reproduce that burst: the initial high-firing response is lost once the spindle has been previously stretched.
Cross-bridge dynamics are believed to underlie history dependence in extrafusal muscle force, and evidence in the literature suggests the same mechanism may operate in the spindle. This model is built on that premise: it models all fiber types — extrafusal, bag, and chain — using cross-bridge mechanics, with different parameter sets for each fiber type to capture their distinct mechanical properties.


Model architecture and biophysics
Model inputs are muscle tendon unit (MTU) length, alpha motor activation, and gamma motor activations (dynamic and static). Because the spindle fibers are in parallel with the fascicle rather than the whole MTU, the model first computes fascicle length from a force balance between the fascicle and the tendon. Fascicle length differs from MTU length because alpha motor activation changes fascicle stiffness, so the intrafusal fibers experience fascicle-level length changes rather than MTU-level changes directly.
Percent activation (0–100%) is internally converted to calcium concentration expressed as pCa (= −log₁₀[Ca²⁺]). A pCa of 4.5 corresponds to 100% activation; a pCa of 9 corresponds to 0% activation.
The cross-bridge model computes force from each intrafusal fiber type. Yank — the rate of change of force — is computed from the bag fiber only. Negative yank values are discarded via half-wave rectification before the signals are combined. A weighted sum of force and (rectified) yank from the intrafusal fibers produces the receptor potential.
To convert receptor potential to a firing rate, the model passes the signal through a basic integrate-and-fire function that performs a cumulative integral of the voltage and generates one spike per fixed number of time steps. The model runs at a 1 ms time step (1000 Hz), which imposes a ceiling of 250 spikes per second on the output. The tutorial graphical user interface outputs receptor potential rather than firing rate, so that users can explore a wider parameter range without hitting that ceiling.


Using the model: forward simulation and optimization
The model requires MATLAB 2020A or later and the Signal Processing Toolbox.
For a forward simulation, users supply MTU length (or fascicle length directly, if available), alpha motor activation, and gamma motor activations. Because gamma motor activity is rarely if ever directly measured in experiments, users who lack that signal can either sweep across a range of gamma activation values to explore the model’s sensitivity, or use the built-in optimization mode.
In optimization mode, the user provides a measured 1A afferent firing record. The optimizer iteratively guesses gamma motor activations, runs a forward simulation to predict spindle firing, and minimizes the difference between predicted and measured firing. The default solver is fmincon, a gradient-based optimizer; pattern search, a non-gradient alternative, is also available.
Model parameters were estimated from optical and molecular characterization of intrafusal fibers — including myosin isoform composition — and from fitting to 1A afferent firing recorded from anesthetized rats and cats. Direct mechanical testing of intrafusal fibers has not been performed because they are too small, so the parameter estimates rely on indirect characterization and electrophysiological recordings.

title: Best practices for scientific programming
text:
Overview

Why Programming Practices Matter in Science
Dr. Finley opens by framing the importance of good programming practices using a “house of cards” analogy: scientific work can be elegant but fragile when built on weak foundations. He describes two recurring failure modes from his own career. First, as a graduate student, he submitted a paper, received reviewer feedback months later requesting reanalysis, and found his files too disorganized to work with efficiently. Second, as a faculty member, he has experienced situations where a student defended or left the lab and the remaining data and code were difficult for anyone else to use. These experiences directly motivated the practices described in this workshop.


Phases of a Programming Workflow
Finley distinguishes two broad phases in scientific programming. The first is a prototyping phase, in which the goal is to explore data and get things working quickly — adding test cases and analyses to a single script, reusing existing code, and accepting something that works for the moment. The second is a development phase, in which code is refined to be robust, well-documented, and shareable. He notes that researchers often remain in the prototyping phase indefinitely, and that a key discipline of the workshop is knowing when and how to transition to higher-quality code. He also briefly mentions a third phase — sharing work publicly — noting that data funded by public money should ultimately be made available to the community, but that this requires adequate documentation and archiving.


Documenting Your Experimental Protocol
Before data collection begins, Finley recommends writing a detailed experimental protocol in a Word document or Google Doc. The protocol should list every step of the experiment, including verbatim instructions given to participants, consent procedures, and screenshots of relevant software settings. Finley states he has never seen an experimental protocol that is too detailed. The goal is that a new lab member, already familiar with basic equipment, should be able to follow the protocol step by step without additional guidance. He also recommends having another student attempt to execute a new protocol as a way to identify steps that are not well defined.


File Organization and Naming Conventions
Finley recommends defining a folder structure for each study before data collection begins. A typical structure might include separate folders for individual subjects, group data, analysis scripts, and papers or presentations. Once the structure is defined, it should be applied consistently across all participants. File names should be machine-readable: no spaces, consistent capitalization, and a consistent number of digits for numerical IDs. On the last point, he explains that without leading zeros, a file system will sort “subject11” before “subject2” because it compares character by character. For date stamps, he recommends year-month-day format with 24-hour time. He also emphasizes that participant names or initials must never appear in file names, as this would make the data identifiable and would no longer be HIPAA compliant.


Metadata, README Files, and Off-Boarding
Supporting documentation — referred to as metadata — should accompany all data. Finley recommends plain-text README files that describe variable coding, units, omitted items in clinical assessments, and other details that cannot easily be embedded in standard data files. He notes that well-maintained metadata allow a researcher to return to data collected years earlier and get up to speed quickly. He also describes an off-boarding checklist he instituted in his lab, which requires graduating students to organize all physical documents (consent forms, data collection sheets), digital data, experiment code, and analysis scripts, and to review them with Finley before he signs off on their dissertation defense. He describes this as a requirement for graduation in his group.


Knowing Your Data
Before writing analysis code, Finley recommends developing a clear understanding of four aspects of your data: how the data were collected (protocol, hardware, and any factors that might influence data properties); the sampling frequency, especially for time-series data such as force, EMG, or marker position; the units of each variable (confusion between meters and millimeters, or degrees and radians, is a common and consequential error); and the file format. On formats, he distinguishes interoperable formats — CSV, Excel, and JSON, which can be read across programming languages and statistical software — from proprietary formats such as MATLAB’s MAT files and motion-capture C3D files, which may not be readable outside their native software.


Building a Data Analysis Pipeline
Finley outlines a data analysis pipeline that moves from data import through quality control, preprocessing, computation of summary measures, figure creation, and statistical analysis. He recommends that the bulk of these steps be automated rather than executed manually. He illustrates this with a four-script MATLAB pipeline shared with workshop participants: the scripts are numbered to indicate run order and named with action verbs — simulate data, combine data, summarize data, and create figures. He also recommends analyzing the first participant’s complete dataset before collecting all participants’ data, because doing so frequently reveals weaknesses or gaps in the pipeline that can be corrected before large-scale data collection begins.


Writing Readable and Reusable Code
Finley offers several practical recommendations for code quality. He advises against single-letter variable names such as x, y, i, or j, recommending instead that names reflect what the variable represents — for example, naming a loop variable “participant” rather than “i” when cycling through participants. He recommends breaking complex operations across multiple lines rather than writing long single-line expressions. He also cautions strongly against copying and pasting code blocks and changing variable names: this practice increases the probability of introducing hard-to-detect errors, because the code will run and may produce a plausible result even when a name has been missed. The recommended alternative is to write functions. MATLAB includes a refactoring feature that converts selected lines of code into a local function by right-clicking and selecting “convert to a local function,” which Finley demonstrates in the workshop. A local function is appropriate when the operation is unlikely to be needed in other scripts; if the function may be reused across projects, it should be saved as a separate function file.


Verifying Code Correctness
Finley emphasizes that a lack of error messages does not guarantee correct results. He illustrates this with a code example in which the same variable is plotted on both axes of a figure: the script produces no errors and the result looks plausible (an upward trend), but the figure is wrong — once the correct variable is placed on the y-axis, the trend disappears. He recommends unit testing as a formal way to verify correctness: writing test code that supplies known inputs to a function and checks whether the output matches the expected value. MATLAB provides a tutorial course on unit testing that Finley recommends. He also briefly describes version control, explaining that the simplest approach is to save a working script under a new name before making changes, so that the prior version is preserved. He notes that GitHub is a more formal tool for version control and code sharing, though he does not cover it in depth in this workshop.


Q&A: MATLAB Compared to Other Languages
During the Q&A portion of the workshop, an attendee asked about using MATLAB versus other languages. Finley noted that the majority of the movement science and biomechanics community still uses MATLAB, while researchers in neuroimaging have largely moved to Python. He described MATLAB as easy to teach, with centralized and well-organized documentation resources. He also noted that data can be exported as CSV or plain-text files regardless of which language is used for analysis, making data sharing possible across communities even when code cannot be directly reused.

title: Material properties in biomechanics
text:
Overview

Introduction: From Frog Tongues to Muscle Mechanics
Dr. Nishikawa opened by noting that, while the workshop title refers to material properties in biomechanics, the content focuses specifically on material properties in muscle mechanics — a distinction she made after observing that standard searches on the topic emphasize bone, cartilage, and tendon while largely omitting muscle. Her interest in muscle material properties grew out of earlier research on how frogs and toads use projectile tongues to catch fast-moving prey. In these animals, the jaw-opening muscles reach their maximum length when the mouth is fully closed, so they cannot be actively pre-stretched. Despite this constraint, the muscles must store and release energy at very high rates. Understanding where that energy is stored in muscle — and how — forms the central question of the talk. The workshop proceeded from first principles (springs and dampers) through to current experimental work on tunable viscoelastic muscle mechanics.


Springs, Dampers, and the Foundations of Viscoelasticity
A linear spring obeys Hooke’s Law: the restoring force F equals the spring constant k multiplied by displacement x (F = kx). In normalized, material-independent form this is written as stress = elastic modulus times strain (σ = Eε). Stiffer materials have a higher spring constant and elastic modulus; more compliant materials have lower values. At small strains many materials behave in a Hookian (linear) way, but at high strain they yield and no longer return to their original shape. A damper (or dashpot) represents viscous resistance: the force it exerts is proportional not to displacement but to the rate of displacement (F = bẋ, where b is the damping constant). A corresponding normalized form relates stress to strain rate through a damping modulus. Both spring and damper properties scale consistently from the whole-muscle level down to the level of individual thick filaments and titin molecules within a sarcomere, because they depend on material composition rather than absolute size.


Viscoelastic Models: From Two to Four Elements
Combining springs and dampers produces viscoelastic models whose behavior depends on how the elements are arranged. The Maxwell model places a spring and a damper in series: stress is equal in both elements but strain is distributed unequally between them. Under a step increase in strain, the Maxwell model produces an initial large force that decays all the way to zero over time. The Kelvin-Voigt model places a spring and a damper in parallel: strain is equal in both elements and total stress equals the sum of the elastic and viscous contributions (σ = Eε + bε̇). Under a step increase in strain, the Kelvin-Voigt model shows a transient force increase that decays down to the residual elastic force in the spring rather than to zero. The Hill model places a spring in series with a Kelvin-Voigt element. More complex arrangements — two Maxwell elements in parallel, two Kelvin-Voigt elements in series, five or more element combinations — are also possible and each produces distinct force-strain behavior. The time constant of a Kelvin-Voigt element, τ, equals the damping modulus divided by the elastic modulus and governs how quickly force decays after a perturbation.


Measuring Viscoelastic Properties: Three Experimental Approaches
Three experimental protocols are commonly used to characterize viscoelastic properties in muscle. In a ramp stretch and hold, the muscle is stretched at a defined amplitude and velocity and then held at the new length; this approach mimics some in-vivo perturbations and allows efficient testing across multiple lengths and activation levels, but velocity transients at the start and end of the ramp mean the muscle is probed across a range of velocities, not just the nominal one, making model fitting complex. Sinusoidal perturbations oscillate muscle length at defined frequencies; elastic forces are in phase with the oscillation and viscous forces are 90 degrees out of phase, which is useful for decomposing the two contributions, but each activation level and starting length must be probed separately, increasing experimental time and fatigue risk. White noise perturbations vary muscle length randomly within a chosen frequency band, permitting multiple frequencies to be assessed simultaneously; they still require separate activation-level and starting-length conditions, but reduce total experiment time compared to sinusoidal methods. Kirsch, Boskov, and Rymer (1994; IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering) applied all three paradigms to cat soleus in a decerebrate preparation and compared how well a single Kelvin-Voigt element, a Hill model, and a standard viscoelastic solid (Maxwell element in parallel with a spring) fit the resulting data. No single model fit both the ramp-stretch and white-noise data sets: the Kelvin-Voigt element fit the white-noise data but not the ramp data at smaller amplitudes; the 3-parameter models fit ramp data but not white noise. The best-fitting model explained only 80–85% of force variance, which falls below the standard set by modern methods.


System Identification in Mouse and Frog Muscles
To identify a better viscoelastic model of muscle, Dr. Nishikawa and collaborators conducted ramp-stretch experiments across the full physiological range of muscle lengths in mouse soleus (ex vivo; stretch amplitude 5% L₀, velocity 1 L₀/s; starting lengths from 0.8 to 1.25 L₀ in 5% increments; n = 7–9 muscles per group) and in three bullfrog muscles (sartorius, iliofibularis, and semitendinosus). Three titin genotypes of mouse soleus were included: wild type, the naturally occurring Mdm spontaneous mutant (primary deletion of approximately 50 amino acids at the boundary of the N2A and PEVK regions of titin), and a transgenic mouse carrying a large deletion spanning exons 112 to 158 of PEVK titin — removing more than 1,500 amino acids, approximately 75% of the contour length of the passive PEVK spring. For each muscle, ramp stretches were performed both passively and at the plateau of isometric force. System identification showed that a model consisting of two Kelvin-Voigt elements in series fit all mouse and frog muscle data with high R-squared values and residuals on the order of 10⁻⁴. The only exception was the exon 112–158 transgenic mouse, whose unusual PEVK structure precluded a good fit — an exception that strengthens rather than undermines the model.


Titin Subdomain Assignment and Activation-Dependent Tuning
The two Kelvin-Voigt elements (k1/b1 and k2/b2) differ in both their passive behavior and their response to activation, and these differences point to distinct molecular origins within titin. The k1/b1 element, assigned to the PEVK1 and PEVK2 sub-domains of titin near the Z-disc, behaves as an exponential spring passively: its stiffness varies over approximately three orders of magnitude from the shortest to the longest muscle length tested, a hallmark of an entropic spring. Passive time constants for k1/b1 are approximately 100 milliseconds; upon activation they increase to roughly 0.5–1 second, meaning the active muscle can retain force stored in this element across a timescale comparable to a full locomotor cycle. The k2/b2 element, assigned to the PEVK3 sub-domain near the M-line, is less stiff and less damped than k1/b1 in passive muscle (time constants approximately 10 ms). Upon activation, k2/b2 stiffens substantially and transitions from an exponential spring to a linear spring; its time constants actually shorten further (to approximately 5 ms) in active muscle. The contrasting behavior of the two elements — k1/b1 becoming slower and k2/b2 becoming faster with activation — means that active muscle shifts energy storage predominantly into k1/b1 and can retain that energy much longer than passive muscle can. These assignments are corroborated by the pattern of differences between wild-type and Mdm muscles, by frog titin isoform data, and by published single-molecule atomic force microscopy data on titin PEVK sub-domains.


Power, Energy Storage, and Comparison to Prior Literature
Using the estimated stiffnesses from system identification, Dr. Nishikawa calculated the power and energy stored by the two Kelvin-Voigt elements during ramp stretches. Elastic energy stored = ½kx², which can also be written as ½F²/k, and approximately two-thirds of stored elastic energy dissipates within one time constant. For the frog sartorius, total power in the viscoelastic transmission rose from approximately 1 W/kg in passive muscle to approximately 100 W/kg upon activation; for the semitendinosus, from approximately 8 W/kg to approximately 200 W/kg — values that represent substantial fractions of the approximately 250 W/kg maximum power predicted by the force-velocity relationship. Energy stored in active sartorius reached approximately 0.063 P₀L₀ (where P₀ is maximum isometric force and L₀ is optimal length), compared to 0.0034 P₀L₀ passively. This active value is close to the 0.092 P₀L₀ total energy storage reported by Linari, Woledge, and Curtin (2003; Journal of Physiology) from single fibers of frog anterior tibialis — work that found only approximately one-third of stored energy explicable by cross bridges, thick filaments, thin filaments, and tendons combined. During Q&A, an on-the-fly unit conversion expressed these energy values as approximately 15–20 J/kg, which participants noted is non-trivial relative to the range of muscle work reported in the locomotion literature. Mdm muscles, which lack most of PEVK1/PEVK2, store approximately 10 times less energy in the active state than wild-type muscles — a result consistent with the k1/b1 element being the primary energy reservoir during activation.


Broader Implications and Q&A Discussion
In closing, Dr. Nishikawa characterized muscles as tunable, variable transmission-ratio viscoelastic actuators that can harvest energy from environmental loads during stretch and release stored energy to amplify or modify cross-bridge power output. Individual titin domains appear to have been shaped over hundreds of millions of years of evolution to provide specialized mechanical properties spanning orders of magnitude in frequency and force. The workshop concluded with extended Q&A covering several topics: the planned extension of the two-Kelvin-Voigt model to muscle-tendon units (adding a spring in series to represent the external tendon); the differences between fast and slow muscles (EDL vs. soleus share the same PEVK exon expression pattern, but the N2A actin-binding site of titin is located closer to the Z-disc in EDL, which Dr. Nishikawa and collaborator Rick Kessler described as the fast muscle “running in high gear”); the timescales over which stored energy is physiologically meaningful (energy retention lasting through a full gait cycle in the mouse and frog); and the development of open-source Lagrangian dynamics models intended to replace Hill models in simulations by incorporating cross-bridge activation dynamics, N2A actin-binding dynamics, thin-filament titin winding, and the length- and activation-dependent viscoelastic response characterized in this work.

title: Movement exploration
text:
Overview

Measuring functional mobility
The Timed Up and Go (TUG) test is one of the most widely used clinical measures of functional mobility. In the standard protocol, a participant rises from a chair, walks a short distance (3 metres in the original protocol), turns, walks back, and returns to sitting. Its simplicity makes it practical for routine clinical use; however, like many standardised scales, the TUG and related balance assessments can exhibit ceiling and floor effects when applied across populations with widely varying functional capacity. This limits their sensitivity at the extremes of ability — an important consideration when selecting outcome measures for a study.


Markerless pose estimation
Marker-based motion capture has long been a laboratory standard for quantifying joint kinematics, but it places practical limits on where and with whom studies can be conducted. Two software tools — AlphaPose and DeepLabCut — allow researchers to extract joint positions directly from ordinary video footage without attaching physical markers to participants.
AlphaPose uses regional multi-person detection to locate body keypoints in video frames. DeepLabCut, originally developed for animal behaviour research, applies deep learning to track user-defined body parts across video and has since been validated for human biomechanics applications. Both tools lower the barrier for collecting movement data in clinical and naturalistic settings.


Psychophysiological measures and movement-related anxiety
When studying how anxiety influences movement, researchers often supplement behavioural measures with physiological indices. Electrodermal activity (EDA), also known as skin conductance, reflects sympathetic nervous system arousal and is used as an index of anxiety in psychophysiology research, including studies of motor behaviour.
A related clinical construct is kinesiophobia — defined as fear of movement or physical activity resulting from a perceived vulnerability to painful injury or re-injury. Kinesiophobia is a meaningful concern in rehabilitation contexts because it can lead patients to avoid beneficial movement even after physical recovery, prolonging disability beyond what tissue damage alone would predict.


Virtual reality as a research tool for anxiety induction
Studying the effects of fear on gait and balance presents a practical challenge: exposing participants to genuine fall risk in order to provoke anxiety is unsafe and unethical. Virtual reality offers a controlled alternative. Height-simulating VR environments have been used in balance and gait research to induce anxiety without exposing participants to physical fall risk, enabling investigators to measure how anxiety-related physiological and behavioural changes interact with postural control and walking.
This approach allows systematic manipulation of perceived threat level while keeping participants physically safe, making it possible to study anxiety-movement interactions that would otherwise be difficult to investigate under controlled laboratory conditions.

title: Introduction to x-ray diffraction
text:
Overview

Why molecular-scale measurements matter in muscle biology
Muscle is hierarchically organized from the whole organ down to individual protein filaments. At the sarcomere level, the interdigitating arrays of thick filaments (myosin) and thin filaments (actin) span roughly 1–10 micrometers in length and are conserved in size across species from cockroaches to blue whales. This invariant length scale reflects the deep conservation of the molecular machinery of contraction.
At the whole-cell scale, muscles are isovolumetric during contraction — a principle demonstrated by Jan Swammerdam around 1666 (the precise year is difficult to confirm from primary sources, as his results were published posthumously; the mid-1660s is generally accepted in historical accounts: Cobb, M., 2002, Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 3, 395–400. DOI: 10.1038/nrn806). Swammerdam placed a frog muscle inside a sealed, fluid-filled chamber with a capillary indicator at the top, then stimulated the attached nerve. The indicator did not move. Muscle volume does not change during contraction, disproving the prevailing idea that a vital fluid was pumped through the nerves to inflate the muscle.
Isovolumetric behavior at the cell scale, however, does not constrain what happens inside the sarcomere. When a muscle shortens along its long axis, the hexagonal lattice of thick and thin filaments must expand radially. Because those filament-to-filament spacings are in the range of tens of nanometers — far smaller than the wavelength of visible light — a light microscope cannot resolve them. Electron microscopy can, but requires chemical fixation and dehydration, giving a static snapshot that may not reflect true spacings in hydrated, functioning muscle. X-ray diffraction fills this gap: it can measure nanometer-scale lattice parameters in living, contracting muscle with millisecond time resolution.


What are X-rays and how do they diffract?
X-rays are electromagnetic waves with wavelengths of approximately 0.1–0.2 nm (1–2 Å), comparable to atomic-scale distances in biological molecules. Wavelengths in this range make X-rays particularly useful for probing molecular structure. When an X-ray beam encounters electrons in matter, each electron reradiates a new scattered wave in many directions. If the scattering centers are arranged in a regular, repeating pattern, the scattered waves from successive repeats can add together or cancel depending on the direction of observation.
At most angles, waves from different repeats arrive with mixed phase relationships and largely cancel (destructive interference), producing little signal. At a specific set of angles, the path difference between waves from successive planes is exactly a whole number of wavelengths, so waves arrive in phase and reinforce (constructive interference), producing a sharp, bright reflection. This condition is Bragg’s law:
\[n\lambda = 2d\sin\theta\]
where λ is the X-ray wavelength, d is the spacing between repeating planes, θ is the angle between the beam and those planes, and n is an integer. In muscle experiments the diffraction angles are very small (well under 1°), allowing a small-angle approximation: measuring the distance S from the beam center to a reflection on a detector placed a known distance L from the sample gives d = λL/S directly. Reflections closer to the beam center correspond to larger real-space spacings; reflections further away correspond to smaller spacings. This inverse relationship between detector-space position and real-space dimension — called reciprocal space — is central to reading any diffraction pattern.
Photo 51, the X-ray diffraction image produced by Rosalind Franklin and Raymond Gosling in 1952, illustrates the power of this approach: the characteristic “X” pattern of crossed arcs was direct evidence that DNA has a helical structure (Franklin & Gosling, 1953, Nature, 171, 740–741. DOI: 10.1038/171740a0). Muscle is also a fibrous, ordered system, and the same physical principles apply.


The myofilament lattice as a quasi-crystal
Within each sarcomere, thick and thin filaments form a regular hexagonal lattice that repeats across thousands of unit cells in the fiber cross-section. Muscle is not a perfect crystal, but its regularity is sufficient for coherent diffraction — scattered waves from parallel planes accumulate to produce distinct reflections on a detector.
When an X-ray beam passes along the fiber axis, it illuminates many myofibrils simultaneously, and those myofibrils are randomly rotated around the beam axis. The diffraction pattern is therefore rotationally averaged: rather than discrete spots, reflections appear as arcs at characteristic distances from the beam center. The horizontal axis of the detector is called the equator; the vertical axis is called the meridian. Equatorial reflections report the lateral arrangement of filaments in cross-section, while meridional reflections and off-meridional layer lines report repeating structures along the filament axis.


Equatorial reflections: reading the cross-sectional lattice
Equatorial reflections arise from repeating planes in the hexagonal cross-sectional lattice. Planes are labeled with Miller indices (h, k). The (1,0) planes give rise to the I(1,0) reflection and the (1,1) planes give rise to the I(1,1) reflection — typically the strongest reflections in the pattern. The center-to-center distance between neighboring thick filaments, D10, is calculated from the position of the I(1,0) reflection using the small-angle Bragg relation. Representative values are approximately 40–45 nm for insect and vertebrate muscle under relaxed conditions, varying with activation state and sarcomere length.
The relative intensities of the equatorial reflections depend not only on lattice spacings but on the distribution of protein mass within the unit cell — specifically, where thin filaments sit relative to thick filaments. In vertebrate skeletal muscle, thin filaments are positioned at trigonal points within the hexagonal lattice (equidistant from three surrounding thick filaments), giving a 2:1 thin-to-thick filament ratio and making I(1,0) and I(1,1) the dominant equatorial features (Franzini-Armstrong & Peachey, 1981, J Cell Biol, 91, 166s–186s. DOI: 10.1083/jcb.91.3.166s). In insect fibrillar flight muscle, a different filament arrangement produces a 3:1 thin-to-thick ratio; the I(1,0) and (2,0) reflections are prominent while I(1,1) is comparatively weak.
Because myosin heads move radially toward actin when they form cross-bridges, the mass distribution within the unit cell shifts during activation. The I(1,1)/I(1,0) intensity ratio is the standard indicator of cross-bridge attachment in the vertebrate muscle literature: as more heads bind, I(1,0) decreases and I(1,1) increases, reflecting the transfer of mass from the thick-filament region outward toward actin (Haselgrove & Huxley, 1973, J Mol Biol, 77, 549–568. DOI: 10.1016/0022-2836(73)90222-2; Millman, 1998, Physiol Rev, 78, 359–391. DOI: 10.1152/physrev.1998.78.2.359).
The most celebrated specimen for insect flight muscle X-ray diffraction is Lethocerus — the giant water bug (Order Hemiptera, Family Belostomatidae), sometimes called a toe-biter or electric light bug. Its flight muscle is among the most crystalline of any animal specimen ever characterized by this technique, a property that has made it the standard for high-resolution insect muscle diffraction studies since the 1960s (Reedy, 1968, J Mol Biol, 31, 155–176. DOI: 10.1016/0022-2836(68)90437-3).


Meridional reflections and layer lines: axial and helical structure
Muscle is ordered in three dimensions. Along the filament axis, both thick and thin filaments have repeating helical structures that produce reflections near or on the meridian, and off-meridional features called layer lines.
Myosin heads project from the thick filament in levels called crowns, spaced approximately 14.3 nm apart along the filament axis. This regular axial repeat produces the strong M3 meridional reflection, along with higher-order reflections M6 and M15 (Huxley & Brown, 1967, J Mol Biol, 30, 383–434. DOI: 10.1016/S0022-2836(67)80046-9). Changes in M3 intensity and position during contraction report on the displacement and strain of myosin heads in real time.
F-actin is described as a 13/6 helix: approximately 13 actin monomers span 6 turns of the long-pitch, left-handed genetic helix (Holmes et al., 1990, Nature, 347, 44–49. DOI: 10.1038/347044a0). The full pseudo-repeat spanning those 13 monomers has a spacing of approximately 36.0–36.5 nm. Note that the ~38.5 nm repeat sometimes seen in muscle diffraction is a distinct structural parameter arising from the tropomyosin/troponin regulatory protein repeat, not from the actin helix geometry itself (Egelman et al., 1982, Nature, 298, 131–135. DOI: 10.1038/298131a0). The pitch of the long-pitch helix is approximately 5.9 nm, producing actin layer line 6 (A6). The complementary right-handed helix contributes a spacing of approximately 5.1 nm at actin layer line 7 (A7). These layer lines appear as off-meridional features in diffraction patterns from well-ordered muscles. When a muscle is stretched, the increased actin filament extension shifts these layer lines slightly inward on the detector, reflecting the larger real-space spacing.


Performing experiments at a synchrotron beamline
Conventional laboratory X-ray sources lack the photon flux to observe weak reflections or capture rapid structural changes in living muscle. Synchrotron facilities overcome this by accelerating electrons near the speed of light in a large storage ring and harvesting extremely intense X-ray beams from those electrons.
The Advanced Photon Source (APS) at Argonne National Laboratory — home to the BioCAT beamline used for many muscle diffraction experiments — has a storage ring approximately 350 m in diameter (circumference ~1.1 km, about two-thirds of a mile). The intense undulator radiation is passed through a silicon monochromator (Si-111) that selects a single wavelength, producing a focused, coherent beam. This beam is directed through a hydrated muscle specimen to a detector placed 3–5 m away. The angular range needed to capture equatorial reflections from lattice spacings of 40–50 nm is less than 1°, which is why the technique is called small-angle X-ray diffraction.
Because synchrotron beams are so intense, modern detectors can record complete diffraction patterns at millisecond time resolution — fast enough to follow structural changes through a single twitch contraction. Muscle specimens are kept hydrated and physiologically active during measurement. Force transducers record mechanical output simultaneously, allowing direct comparison of molecular structural changes with macroscopic mechanics. Depending on the experiment, specimens range from single dissected fiber bundles to whole small animals or insects placed directly in the beam path.


From molecular structure to whole-muscle function: a case study
A central question in integrative muscle biology is whether nanometer-scale differences in myofilament lattice geometry can explain macroscopic differences in mechanical output. A well-studied example involves the cockroach leg. Two muscles — numbered 178 and 179 — act on the same joint, share a single motor neuron (forming effectively one motor unit), and have the same mass, moment arm, and virtually identical force-length and force-velocity curves. By every standard mechanical characterization they appear identical. Yet work loop experiments reveal that one muscle acts as a net positive work producer (a motor) while the other acts as a net energy absorber (a brake). This functional distinction was first characterized in depth by Ahn & Full (2002, J Exp Biol, 205, 379–389. DOI: 10.1242/jeb.205.3.379).
Because the steady-state mechanical properties of the two muscles are the same, any structural difference must emerge only under the dynamic conditions of cyclic contraction. Subsequent time-resolved synchrotron X-ray diffraction experiments at the APS beamline — combining lattice spacing measurements with simultaneous work loop protocols — identified differences in myofilament lattice structure between the two muscles. Spatially explicit computational models incorporating lattice geometry can qualitatively reproduce different work loop shapes from muscles with otherwise identical intrinsic cross-bridge kinetics, providing a mechanistic bridge between molecular structure and organ-level mechanics.
This example illustrates the unique capability of time-resolved synchrotron X-ray diffraction: it can detect structural differences invisible to conventional mechanical assays, and it operates at the length and time scales where molecular mechanisms determine whole-muscle function.

title: Introduction to muscle anatomy and physiology
text:
Overview

The Conserved and Versatile Muscular System
The muscular system is one of the most highly conserved systems across the animal kingdom. The fundamental organization of muscle, the mechanisms of force generation, and the responses to changes in length and activation level are remarkably similar from insects to large mammals (Burkholder & Lieber, 2001). This conservation allows researchers to identify common principles and make broad comparative claims about muscle function across species.
At the same time, muscles are versatile and adaptive. A muscle can function not only as a motor—generating mechanical work to power movement—but also as a spring (storing and returning elastic energy), a brake (absorbing energy during active lengthening), or a strut (transmitting force while changing length minimally). Subtle differences in muscle structure, protein isoform expression, architecture, or neural control can substantially alter whole-animal performance. Understanding muscle function therefore requires considering both its conserved principles and the specializations that adapt it to particular behaviors.


Sarcomere Structure and Hierarchical Organization
Skeletal muscle is organized hierarchically. The whole muscle is composed of fascicles, which contain individual muscle fibers. A single muscle fiber is a multinucleated cell that can span the entire length of the muscle. Within each fiber, myofibrils run longitudinally, and each myofibril is composed of repeating contractile units called sarcomeres.
The sarcomere is the fundamental unit of force generation. In vertebrates, sarcomere resting length is typically 2.0–2.5 µm, a dimension that is highly conserved across species (Gordon et al., 1966; Burkholder & Lieber, 2001). The sarcomere is bounded at each end by the Z-disc. Thin filaments (composed primarily of actin) extend inward from each Z-disc. Thick filaments (composed of myosin) are anchored at the M-line at the center of the sarcomere. Myosin molecules project cross-bridge heads that can bind to actin and undergo a power stroke, drawing the thin filaments toward the center and shortening the sarcomere.
A third filament, titin, connects the Z-disc to the M-line and provides passive stiffness to the sarcomere. Titin functions as a molecular spring and is responsible for much of the passive elastic resistance felt when a resting muscle is stretched (Labeit & Kolmerer, 1995).
Sarcomere dimensions can vary substantially in invertebrates. Obliquely striated muscles found in some invertebrates—including nematodes and other soft-bodied animals—can elongate substantially beyond the range of vertebrate striated muscle while still maintaining force, a property termed superelongation (Rosenbluth, 1967). This extended operating range contrasts with the narrower force-generating range of typical vertebrate sarcomeres.


Excitation-Contraction Coupling
Excitation-contraction coupling (ECC) refers to the sequence of events linking an action potential at the muscle fiber membrane to mechanical contraction at the sarcomere. An action potential propagates along the sarcolemma and into the T-tubule network, triggering calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) through ryanodine receptor channels. The rapid rise in intracellular calcium concentration causes calcium to bind to troponin on the thin filament, inducing a conformational change that exposes myosin-binding sites on actin. Myosin cross-bridges then attach and cycle, generating force and shortening (Bers, 2002).
Relaxation occurs as calcium is pumped back into the SR by SERCA (sarcoplasmic/endoplasmic reticulum Ca²⁺-ATPase) pumps—an energy-requiring process. Because calcium reuptake is slower than its release, the time to full relaxation is longer than the time to peak force development. This kinetic asymmetry underlies temporal summation: if a second stimulus arrives before the muscle has fully relaxed, the resulting twitches sum to produce greater force.
ECC kinetics vary across muscle types and species. Muscles that contract at high frequencies have higher SR density and faster Ca²⁺ cycling machinery than slow muscles (Berchtold et al., 2000). The distinction between fast-twitch and slow-twitch fibers reflects, in part, differences in the molecular components governing ECC speed and the rate of calcium handling.


Force-Frequency Relationship
The force output of a muscle is strongly influenced by the frequency at which motor neurons stimulate it. At low stimulation frequencies, each stimulus produces a discrete twitch and the muscle fully relaxes between contractions. As frequency increases, successive twitches begin to overlap before relaxation is complete—a phenomenon called summation. At intermediate frequencies, incomplete tetanus produces a rippled, elevated force plateau. At high frequencies, twitches fuse completely into a smooth, sustained contraction called fused tetanus, which represents the maximum force the muscle can generate under those conditions (Lieber, 2002).
The force-frequency relationship arises from calcium dynamics: higher stimulation frequencies allow calcium to accumulate in the cytosol, activating more cross-bridges and increasing force. Force production reaches a ceiling at fused tetanus, constrained by the total number of available cross-bridges and sarcomere geometry.
In intact animals, the nervous system dynamically modulates stimulation frequency (rate coding) to regulate force output. Motor unit recruitment and firing rate interact to produce the graded forces seen in natural movements. Simple isometric force-frequency measurements do not fully capture this complexity—brief, high-frequency bursts followed by lower frequencies (doublet potentiation) can enhance force beyond what steady-state measurements predict.


Force-Length Relationship
The force a muscle can generate depends on the length at which it is activated. The active force-length curve follows an inverted-U shape, peaking at an optimal length (L₀) where cross-bridge overlap between thick and thin filaments is greatest. At shorter lengths, steric interference reduces the number of productive cross-bridges. At longer lengths, overlap diminishes, fewer cross-bridges can form, and active force declines (Gordon et al., 1966). Passive force also increases with length, primarily due to the elastic properties of titin and the extracellular matrix, so the total force at any length is the sum of active and passive contributions.
The shape and operating range of the force-length curve differ across species. Many vertebrate muscles operate near the descending limb during natural movements, but some invertebrate muscles have much broader curves. Species with large sarcomeres can maintain force over a much wider range of lengths, allowing behaviors that require extreme limb or body excursions. Some chameleon tongue retractor muscles are classified as super-contracting: the proposed mechanism allows thick filaments to pass through gaps in the Z-disc and interact with thin filaments of adjacent sarcomeres, enabling force generation at extremely short lengths (Herrel et al., 2001). It is important to note that the accelerator muscles of the chameleon tongue operate through a different mechanism—elastic energy storage and release—rather than supercontraction.
The force-length relationship is a quasi-static measure obtained under isometric conditions. Natural movements involve dynamic length changes, and muscle force during active stretching or shortening can deviate substantially from predictions based on this static curve alone.


Force-Velocity Relationship and Muscle Architecture
The force a muscle generates during active shortening decreases with increasing shortening velocity—the force-velocity relationship. At maximum shortening velocity (V_max), the muscle produces no net force. As velocity decreases toward zero (isometric), force rises to its maximum. This relationship reflects cross-bridge cycling kinetics: at higher velocities, myosin heads have less time to remain attached and generate force (Hill, 1938). Power output—the product of force and velocity—peaks at an intermediate shortening velocity (approximately one-third of V_max in many vertebrate muscles; Josephson, 1993), then declines toward both extremes.
The force-velocity relationship varies with fiber type. Fast-twitch fibers have higher myosin ATPase activity, faster cross-bridge cycling rates, and higher V_max than slow-twitch fibers, and thus reach higher peak power. This relationship has been characterized across species with diverse locomotor demands.
Muscle architecture—the arrangement of fibers relative to the line of action—also determines the force and velocity characteristics of a whole muscle. In parallel-fibered muscles, fibers run roughly parallel to the tendon, placing more sarcomeres in series and maximizing shortening speed and excursion. In pennate muscles, fibers attach at an angle (the pennation angle) to the central tendon. This geometry allows more fibers to be packed into a given volume, increasing physiological cross-sectional area and, consequently, maximum force production, at some cost to shortening velocity (Lieber & Fridén, 2000). Comparative studies of frog species illustrate this principle: muscles specialized for swimming show different relationships between cross-sectional area and fiber length compared with muscles specialized for jumping or walking.
The force-velocity relationship is typically measured under isotonic conditions with maximal activation—conditions that poorly represent the submaximal, dynamically changing activation and length conditions of natural movements. History-dependent effects (such as increased force following active stretch) and contributions of elastic structures such as titin are not captured by this relationship.


Titin as a Tunable Viscoelastic Spring
Titin is the largest known protein and the third filament of the sarcomere, spanning continuously from the Z-disc to the M-line (Labeit & Kolmerer, 1995). Its mechanical properties help maintain sarcomere structural integrity and contribute to both passive and active muscle mechanics.
The I-band region of titin—the segment that extends when the sarcomere is elongated—contains mechanically distinct regions. The tandem immunoglobulin (Ig) domain segment acts as a compliant spring at low forces, straightening progressively as the sarcomere is stretched. The PEVK domain (named for its high content of proline, glutamate, valine, and lysine residues) contributes the steeper, exponential rise in passive force at longer sarcomere lengths (Granzier & Labeit, 2004). The N2A element, positioned between these spring regions, is a unique sequence. Both the tandem Ig segment and the PEVK domain are sites of alternative splicing that generate titin isoforms of different lengths and stiffnesses (Labeit & Kolmerer, 1995; Buck et al., 2014).
Evidence from in vitro and in situ experiments supports the hypothesis that the N2A region of titin can interact with actin in a calcium-dependent manner, stiffening titin during active muscle contraction (Dutta et al., 2018; Nishikawa, 2020). If confirmed, this would mean that calcium activation does not only trigger cross-bridge cycling but also engages titin as an additional active spring, particularly during active stretch. This mechanism is an active area of investigation and is not yet universally accepted as established.
In vertebrates, titin is encoded by a single gene (TTN) that undergoes extensive alternative splicing to produce isoforms differing in length and composition (Labeit & Kolmerer, 1995). Long titin isoforms, as found in the soleus, confer lower passive stiffness. Shorter isoforms, as found in the psoas, confer higher passive stiffness (Granzier & Labeit, 2004). This isoform variation allows muscles with different mechanical demands within the same organism to tune their passive elastic properties.
In invertebrates such as Drosophila, multiple distinct titin-like genes—including projectin and sallimus (D-titin, encoded by the sls gene)—encode proteins with analogous structural roles (Burkart et al., 2007; Bullard et al., 2005). Rather than diversifying through alternative splicing of a single gene, invertebrates can generate mechanical diversity through expression of multiple distinct genes.
The functional significance of titin isoform variation within an organism is illustrated by studies of muscles with contrasting mechanical roles in the same animal. In toads, the plantaris muscle (which shortens to produce mechanical power during jumping) is mechanically compliant in its passive properties, while the anconeus muscle (which actively lengthens to absorb energy during landing) is substantially stiffer (Azizi, 2014). These passive mechanical differences likely reflect differences in titin isoform expression, though the molecular correspondence requires further investigation.
