title: System identification
text:
Overview

What Is System Identification?
Mathematical modeling in biomechanics follows two broad paradigms. The first derives governing equations from first principles — fundamental physical laws such as Newton’s laws of motion, thermodynamics, or electromagnetism — where every parameter has a known physical interpretation. The second is system identification: the process of building mathematical models of dynamical systems from experimentally measured input-output data. System identification models serve three main purposes: characterizing and analyzing system behavior, predicting system outputs from a given input, and designing controllers that interact with the system.
In practice, models occupy a spectrum. White-box models have high structural fidelity — the governing equations are well established and all parameters are physically interpretable; system identification is used primarily to estimate the unknown parameter values from data. Black-box models rely almost entirely on empirical input-output data with minimal structural assumptions. Gray-box models blend known structure with data-driven parameter estimation. Research on muscle and tendon mechanics typically employs gray- and white-box approaches, where the model topology (for example, a spring-damper network) is informed by physical intuition and the parameters are identified from experiment.
Some useful terminology: a dynamic system is one whose state evolves over time; a static system is at equilibrium. Constitutive models describe how a specific material responds to a physical stimulus (mechanical load, temperature, or electromagnetic field) and may be static or dynamic. Within Newtonian constitutive models, kinematic models describe the geometry of motion, quasi-static models neglect inertial forces relative to viscous and elastic forces, and dynamic models explicitly include inertial effects. Because “dynamic” is used in several senses across disciplines, it is best practice to specify “Newtonian dynamic model” when that is the intended meaning.
The System Identification Toolbox in MATLAB — developed by Lennart Ljung — is the primary computational platform for the analyses described in this workshop. Specialized code written by Rick Castler adapts these general tools to ramp stretch and transfer-function analyses of muscle and tendon.


Mathematical Foundations: Laplace Transforms and Transfer Functions
The equations governing viscoelastic systems are ordinary differential equations (ODEs) in time. A canonical example is the damped oscillator: a mass connected to a spring and a damper, driven by an applied force F. Applying Newton’s second law yields a second-order ODE relating position x(t), velocity ẋ(t), and acceleration ẍ(t) to F(t). Extracting the ratio of output to input directly from such an ODE is algebraically cumbersome because of the time-derivative terms.
The Laplace transform converts a time-domain function f(t) into a function of a complex variable s. In the Laplace domain, differentiation with respect to time becomes multiplication by s, converting the ODE into an algebraic equation. The inverse Laplace transform converts back; in practice, look-up tables of transform pairs handle most cases encountered in biomechanics.
For a linear system with zero initial conditions, the ratio of output to input in the Laplace domain is the transfer function — a rational polynomial in s. The roots of the numerator are the zeros of the transfer function; the roots of the denominator are the poles. Poles and zeros together determine the system’s frequency response, transient behavior, and stability.
A useful practical tool is the analogy between mechanical and electrical systems: for linear systems, velocity is analogous to voltage and force is analogous to current. A spring-damper network can therefore be represented as an equivalent electrical circuit, facilitating analysis and parameter estimation using established tools from electrical engineering.
Model selection — determining how many springs and dampers, and in what configuration — is guided by comparing candidate models using goodness-of-fit metrics (R², RMSE) and information criteria (Akaike Information Criterion, AIC; Bayesian Information Criterion, BIC). Information criteria penalize model complexity, guarding against overfitting: a more complex model will almost always fit data better, but that improvement may reflect noise rather than true system dynamics.


Viscoelastic Building Blocks: Springs, Dampers, and Their Combinations
The fundamental mechanical elements of viscoelastic models are the linear spring and the linear damper.
A linear spring produces a force proportional to displacement: F = kx, where k is the spring constant. This is a static model — it contains no time-varying terms. Normalizing by cross-sectional area (stress) and resting length (strain) yields the familiar stress-strain relationship, which is linear over a material’s elastic range.
A linear damper (analogous to a piston moving through a viscous fluid) produces a force proportional to velocity: F = Bẋ, where B is the damping coefficient. This is a dynamic model because the strain rate (first time-derivative of displacement) is time-varying.
These elements are combined into more complex models:
Maxwell model (spring in series with a damper): stress is equal in both elements; strain is distributed between them. Under a step stretch, force rises during the stretch and then decays to zero — because the damper eventually accommodates the applied displacement. This makes the Maxwell element a fluid: it cannot sustain a static force indefinitely.
Kelvin-Voigt model (spring in parallel with a damper): strain is equal in both elements; stress is distributed. Under a step stretch, an initial force spike from the viscous element decays with time constant τ = B/k, leaving a sustained elastic force. This element can sustain a static force and thus behaves as a solid.
More complex models are built by combining these two-element systems:

Maxwell solid: a spring in parallel with a Maxwell element (three elements total).
Kelvin-Voigt solid: a spring in series with a Kelvin-Voigt element; this structure is structurally similar to the Hill muscle model.
Two Kelvin-Voigt elements in series: the model consistently identified for skeletal muscle across multiple species and preparations.
Two or more elements in parallel or series: explored when simpler models fail to fit the data, with model selection guided by AIC/BIC.

Empirical findings from this laboratory’s system identification work indicate that skeletal muscles (cat soleus, frog sartorius and semitendinosus, rat medial gastrocnemius, and a range of mouse muscles) are consistently described by two Kelvin-Voigt elements in series, while tendons (rat tail) are described by a Kelvin-Voigt solid.


Experimental Identification of Viscoelastic Models
Three experimental protocols can be used to probe viscoelastic properties, with length as the input and force as the output:

Ramp stretch and hold: the tissue is stretched at a controlled rate to a fixed length and held. The force response includes a transient spike and subsequent relaxation — characteristic of a Kelvin-Voigt-type element. The corners of the ramp introduce velocity and acceleration transients that effectively sample a range of frequencies, similar to the broadband excitation of white-noise protocols. This approach is most similar to in vivo perturbations (stretch from an antagonist muscle, ground reaction force, or an external mechanical perturbation) and allows systematic sampling across the full physiological length range (approximately 0.8 to 1.2 times optimal length) with minimal fatigue.
Sinusoidal perturbation: a sinusoidal length input is applied at a given frequency; elastic components respond in phase with the input and viscous components respond out of phase, with the phase lag proportional to the element’s time constant.
White noise (pseudorandom) perturbation: random length changes covering a defined amplitude and frequency bandwidth. In principle, all three protocols yield equivalent parameter estimates; they differ in practical advantages and ease of implementation.

Transfer functions for the tendon model (Kelvin-Voigt solid) and muscle model (two Kelvin-Voigt elements in series) are formulated as impedance transfer functions — the ratio of force to velocity in the Laplace domain. The tendon model transfer function has two zeros and one pole; the muscle model has two zeros and two poles. Parameters are estimated by minimizing the sum of squared error between the model response and experimental measurements, using the least-squares method implemented in MATLAB’s System Identification Toolbox.
Passive muscles display a Kelvin-Voigt-like force response (spike followed by exponential decay). Active muscles produce a larger initial force and a slower decay, indicating that activation changes the viscoelastic properties. Specifically, upon stimulation, the second Kelvin-Voigt element (KV2) becomes substantially stiffer, concentrating almost all of the elastic energy storage into the first element (KV1).


Energy Storage, Power Amplification, and Dissipation
Once spring constants k and damping coefficients B are identified, a full mechanical analysis follows analytically for each element:

Energy stored: E = ½kx² = ½F²/k
Power: P = kx²/Δt = F × v (force times velocity)
Time constant: τ = B/k; two-thirds of the viscous force dissipates within τ seconds

Because the two Kelvin-Voigt elements in the muscle model are in series, they share the same force. The element with the lower spring constant therefore stores more energy. In passive muscle, the two elements store energy in similar proportions. Upon activation, KV2 stiffens markedly, storing almost no energy; nearly all elastic energy in the active muscle is concentrated in KV1. This activation-dependent redistribution means one element functions primarily as a power amplifier and the other primarily as a mechanical brake.
These quantities scale with activation and muscle length in ways that connect to whole-animal mechanics. Linari and colleagues (2003) stretched single frog muscle fibers during activation and measured heat and work output using a thermopile, normalizing elastic energy storage to the product of maximum isometric force and optimal length (P₀ · L₀). Their analysis showed that cross-bridges account for only a small fraction of total stored energy, and that the combined contributions of internal connective tissue, thick and thin filament compliance, and passive titin could explain only a portion of the total — leaving a substantial fraction unaccounted for. Energy measurements from frog sartorius muscles using the system identification approach described here, expressed in the same P₀ · L₀ units, yield active-muscle values that correspond closely to this previously unexplained fraction. This convergence suggests that active titin viscoelasticity accounts for the missing energy.
Power amplification and dissipation are observed directly: upon activation of frog sartorius, total positive power increases by approximately two orders of magnitude compared to the passive condition, while KV2 simultaneously increases its dissipative output. These relationships bridge isolated-tissue mechanics to in vivo function.


From Isolated Muscles to Whole-Animal Locomotion
In vivo recordings from guinea fowl running over unexpected obstacles (Monica Daley, University of California, Irvine) illustrate the functional significance of muscle viscoelasticity. Simultaneous measurements of muscle fascicle length (sonomicrometry), tendon force (tendon buckle), and muscle activation (EMG) show that during an unexpected step down into a hole, the muscle force is substantially lower than during a level stride — despite a larger EMG signal. The reverse occurs when the bird steps up: force is amplified relative to the level-stride baseline. Both responses occur faster than neural feedback can operate, implicating the intrinsic mechanical properties of the muscle-tendon unit — particularly titin viscoelasticity — as an automatic stabilization mechanism.
These observations motivate the system identification approach: by characterizing viscoelastic parameters across the full physiological length range and activation state, the isolated-muscle model can predict the energy storage, dissipation, and power amplification that arise during locomotor perturbations. The viscoelastic transmission in the sarcomere may also explain residual force enhancement — the sustained force elevation that persists after active stretch beyond what cross-bridge models predict — as a property of titin rather than of cross-bridge cycling.


Connecting Model Elements to Titin Biology
The two Kelvin-Voigt elements identified by system identification are not purely phenomenological: converging evidence from transgenic and mutant mouse models links them to specific domains of the titin protein.
Titin is the giant elastic protein spanning the half-sarcomere from Z disc to M-line. Its I-band portion contains three functionally distinct elastic segments:
Tandem immunoglobulin (Ig) domains: a series of folded Ig-like domains that behave as an entropic spring, extending under low force with minimal force development. In the viscoelastic model, the tandem Ig region does not contribute substantially as a spring or damper element; it likely limits extension of the PEVK region without itself generating large forces.
PEVK domain: a proline (P), glutamate (E), valine (V), and lysine (K)-rich disordered segment that extends under force. The PEVK domain is the primary structural candidate for the two Kelvin-Voigt elements. Evidence: - A transgenic mouse with a large deletion in titin shows only a single Kelvin-Voigt element in series with a spring — consistent with partial deletion of the PEVK region collapsing two KV elements into one. - A mutant in which a portion of the PEVK region is shorter and stiffer shows a detectable shift in the identified viscoelastic parameters. - The spring constant of passive muscle changes approximately 1,000-fold across the physiological length range (0.8 to 1.2 L₀) — an exponential dependence consistent with titin’s known behavior as an exponential spring. - In slow postural muscles such as soleus, the PEVK domain contains more than 2,000 amino acids, conferring high compliance and late onset of passive tension development. Cardiac titin contains a substantially shorter PEVK domain, consistent with the high passive stiffness of cardiac muscle.
The PEVK domain appears mechanically non-uniform: one sub-domain is specialized for elastic energy storage and power amplification (KV1), while another provides dissipative function (KV2). This partition may reflect evolutionary optimization — one region tuned for energy efficiency during cyclic contractions, the other for damping and injury prevention during high-force eccentric loading.
N2 insertions: isoform-specific elements that modulate the effective spring length and stiffness of the titin molecule. In most skeletal muscles, the N2A element is positioned relatively close to the Z disc, producing a stiffer spring; in soleus, it is positioned farther from the Z disc, contributing to greater compliance. EDL muscles, which have a more proximal N2A position, show a larger increase in stiffness upon activation compared to soleus — consistent with the hypothesis that N2A position controls the sensitivity of titin-actin interactions to calcium. The N2B insertion (found in cardiac titin) adds approximately 40 nm to the tandem Ig region, moving the potential titin-actin interaction site closer to the M-line and increasing compliance relative to N2A skeletal isoforms. The N2BA isoform, present in some cardiac and slow skeletal preparations, contains both N2A and N2B insertions and represents the most compliant major isoform.
Together, these structural differences predict and explain the isoform-dependent variation in viscoelastic parameters identified across frog (sartorius, iliofibularis, semitendinosus), rodent, and cat muscles. System identification provides a quantitative framework for comparing these isoforms functionally and for testing mechanistic hypotheses about how titin architecture shapes muscle performance across species and physiological conditions.

title: Intro to the mechanics of the musculoskeletal system
text:
Overview

Mechanics and its divisions
Mechanics is the field of studying how bodies react to forces acting on them. Within mechanics, two major divisions are relevant to the musculoskeletal system.
In statics, bodies are in equilibrium: the forces acting on them are balanced, and there is no movement — velocity and acceleration are both zero. A person holding a fixed posture represents a static problem in which each body segment is in equilibrium.
In dynamics, the body or its segments are moving. Dynamics is further divided into kinematics, which describes the geometric aspects of motion — position, velocity, and acceleration — without regard to the forces causing that motion, and kinetics, which incorporates the forces responsible for motion.
Loads acting on the body include body weight (mass reacting to gravity), ground reaction forces and contact forces from the environment, and forces from interacting objects such as a handheld weight. When these loads balance, equilibrium is achieved and there is no movement. When they become unbalanced, the body accelerates.


Body segments, joints, and degrees of freedom
The human body is usefully modeled as a system of rigid segments connected at joints. Each segment has its own center of mass and associated inertia; the loads acting on individual segments — and the internal loads at joint interfaces — determine both posture and movement.
Joints define how adjacent segments can move relative to each other. Two key descriptors are degrees of freedom (DOF) — the number of independent ways two segments can move relative to one another — and range of motion, the extent of movement permitted by the joint structures. DOF can be rotational (movement about an axis) or translational (displacement along an axis).
The hip is a ball-and-socket joint providing 3 rotational DOF: flexion/extension, abduction/adduction, and internal/external rotation. The elbow is often simplified as a hinge joint: the humeroulnar articulation behaves approximately as a hinge with 1 DOF (flexion/extension). This is a useful model simplification, but the full elbow complex has 2 functional DOF when forearm rotation is included, because the proximal radioulnar joint — anatomically part of the elbow — adds pronation/supination as a second independent motion. The wrist (radiocarpal joint) has 2 DOF — flexion/extension and radial/ulnar deviation. Forearm pronation/supination occurs at the proximal and distal radioulnar joints and is not a DOF of the wrist joint itself.
By constraining certain DOF, joints generate reaction forces and moments in the directions that motion is not permitted. This is why free body diagrams of individual segments include joint reaction forces and moments as unknowns to be solved from equilibrium.


Internal loads and stress states
When external loads act on a body segment, internal loads develop within the structure. Cutting a cross-section through the structure and applying equilibrium reveals three types of internal load: a normal force perpendicular to the cut surface, shear forces parallel to the cut surface, and moments (bending and torsional) about the cross-sectional axes.
These internal loads produce characteristic stress distributions:

Tension and compression (axial normal force): stress is distributed uniformly across the cross-section, directed perpendicular to the cut surface.
Bending (from a bending moment): the greatest tensile stress develops at the outer fiber on the tension side, the greatest compressive stress at the outer fiber on the compression side, and stress is zero at the neutral axis in the middle. A bone bending under load is longer and in tension on one side, shorter and in compression on the other — the bone cross-section illustrates this distribution directly.
Torsion (from a torsional moment about the longitudinal axis): shear stress is greatest at the outer surface of the structure and approaches zero at the center, because the outermost material must displace the most during twisting.

Stress (σ) is force distributed over an area — in its simplest uniaxial form, σ = F/A. Strain (ε) is the change in length normalized by the original length (ε = ΔL/L₀), a dimensionless quantity often expressed as a percentage. These normalizations allow material behavior to be described independently of specimen geometry.


Material properties of musculoskeletal tissues
In the linear elastic (Hookean) region, stress is proportional to strain: σ = Eε, where Young’s modulus (E) is the proportionality constant and equals the slope of the linear portion of the stress-strain curve. A higher Young’s modulus indicates a stiffer material that requires greater stress to achieve the same deformation.
Musculoskeletal connective tissues display a characteristic nonlinear stress-strain curve with four regions: a low-stiffness toe region, a stiffer linear elastic region, a yield and micro-failure region where progressive structural damage occurs, and ultimate failure. The yield strength and ultimate strength mark the stress levels at which these transitions occur.
Two additional features distinguish biological tissues from idealized isotropic elastic materials:

Anisotropy: mechanical properties differ depending on the direction of loading, owing to the preferential alignment of collagen fibers and mineral crystallites within the tissue. Loading a tendon along its fiber axis versus across it yields dramatically different stress-strain curves.
Viscoelasticity: the stress-strain response depends on the rate of loading (strain rate). Under rapid loading, tissues appear stiffer than under slow loading. Viscoelasticity also manifests as creep, stress relaxation, and hysteresis — behaviors arising from fluid-solid interactions and intrinsic polymer chain dynamics within the tissue.

The structural mechanical properties of a specific anatomical structure depend on both material properties and morphology. A longer ligament with the same material properties and cross-sectional area is less stiff than a shorter one (stiffness k = EA/L); a ligament with a larger cross-sectional area requires greater force to produce the same elongation and is therefore stiffer. Stress and strain normalizations account for these morphological differences when characterizing material properties independent of specimen size.


Bone and cartilage
Bone exists in two tissue forms. Compact (cortical) bone forms the dense outer shell of bones. Trabecular (cancellous) bone forms the inner, porous structure — particularly at the ends of long bones — with an open lattice of bony struts (trabeculae) that distributes load while minimizing mass. At the microscale, cortical bone is organized into osteons (Haversian systems): concentric rings (lamellae) of collagen fibers with mineral content surrounding central canals that house blood vessels and nerve fibers. This oriented microstructure gives bone its anisotropic mechanical properties.
There are three types of cartilage. Articular (hyaline) cartilage lines joint surfaces and reduces friction at articulations; its friction coefficient is among the lowest of any biological surface, achieved through fluid pressurization and glycoprotein boundary lubricants. Elastic cartilage, distinguished by its high elastin content, is found in structures such as the external ear. Fibrocartilage is a dense, stiff tissue found in the menisci and the labra (acetabular and glenoid). Intervertebral discs are composite structures: the annulus fibrosus is fibrocartilaginous, while the nucleus pulposus is a hydrated proteoglycan-rich gel — not fibrocartilage — with a distinct mechanical function of distributing compressive loads through hydrostatic pressure.
The mechanical behavior of cartilage arises largely from its extracellular matrix. Proteoglycans (primarily aggrecan) are hydrophilic macromolecules bearing dense negative fixed charges that attract and retain interstitial fluid through Donnan osmotic pressure. Fluid pressurization under load, together with the tensile load-bearing capacity of the collagen fiber network, is the basis of the viscoelastic behavior characteristic of cartilage. The cell density of connective tissue also governs remodeling capacity: fibrocartilage has low cell density and limited vascularity, which is why injuries to structures such as the meniscus heal slowly.


Tendon, ligament, and muscle mechanics
Tendons connect muscle to bone; ligaments connect bone to bone. Both are dense fibrous connective tissues composed primarily of type I collagen. In tendons, collagen fibers are arranged nearly parallel to one another, optimizing uniaxial tensile load transmission along the tendon axis. In ligaments, fibers are also primarily longitudinally aligned but show slightly greater inter-bundle angular variation, reflecting the multidirectional loading demands of structures that stabilize joints.
The low-stiffness toe region of the tendon and ligament stress-strain curve arises from the progressive recruitment and straightening of initially crimped (wavy) collagen fibers under load. As strain increases, more fibers straighten and begin to bear load, progressively increasing tissue stiffness until all fibers are engaged and the tissue enters the linear elastic region. Beyond the linear region, fibers begin to fail sequentially, reducing stiffness until ultimate failure.
Muscle has passive and active mechanical properties, both characterized empirically. Passive behavior — force generated by a lengthened but unactivated muscle — arises from the extracellular matrix (ECM) and intracellular proteins. Titin, the giant elastic protein spanning the sarcomere’s I-band, is the dominant intracellular contributor to passive stiffness; titin also contributes to active force through calcium-dependent interactions with actin. Active force is generated by the sarcomeric contractile proteins (actin and myosin). The active force-length relationship, force-velocity relationship, and passive force-length curve are the core empirical descriptors of muscle mechanics; they cannot be derived analytically from first principles and are parameterized from experimental data.
With aging, increased ECM content (collagen crosslinking and accumulation) and intramuscular fat infiltration alter passive mechanical properties and reduce contractile tissue fraction. Muscle hypertrophy occurs through an increase in muscle fiber cross-sectional area — expansion of existing fibers through accretion of myofibrillar proteins — rather than through a meaningful increase in fiber number.


Experimental characterization and computational modeling
Because the material properties of musculoskeletal tissues arise from their microstructure, they cannot generally be derived analytically; they are characterized empirically through mechanical testing. A typical approach applies controlled deformation to a tissue specimen using a uniaxial testing machine while measuring force, then converts force to stress and elongation to strain to construct stress-strain curves. Tissue samples can be loaded along or across the primary fiber direction to capture anisotropic behavior, or tested at different loading rates to characterize viscoelastic rate-dependence.
Testing configurations range from ex vivo specimens (cadaveric or animal tissue removed from its native context) to in situ setups that preserve more physiologically relevant boundary conditions and combined load states. Converting measured force and elongation to stress and strain requires accurate measurement of cross-sectional area and original length — a nontrivial requirement for irregularly shaped biological structures.
Where direct mechanical measurement is impractical, computational modeling allows forces and stresses to be estimated under complex loading conditions. FEBio (Finite Elements for Biomechanics) is an open-source finite element solver designed specifically for biological materials, supporting hyperelastic, viscoelastic, biphasic, and multiphasic constitutive formulations suited to musculoskeletal tissues (Maas et al., 2012, PMID 22482660). Constitutive models — the mathematical definitions of nonlinear, anisotropic, viscoelastic tissue behavior — require high-fidelity experimental measurements as inputs, linking the empirical characterization of tissue properties directly to computational prediction of in vivo mechanics.

title: EMG filtering
text:
Overview

Introduction to Filter Theory
EMG signals are recorded in the time domain, but filter design is grounded in the frequency domain. The underlying principle is that any signal can be theoretically reconstructed as a sum of sine waves at different frequencies and amplitudes. A filter exploits this property by selectively attenuating components at certain frequency ranges while leaving others unchanged. The frequencies preserved are called the pass band, and those removed fall in the stop band.
A Bode plot is a standard tool for visualizing filter behavior. It displays the magnitude of the filtered signal (often in decibels) as a function of frequency, allowing you to see how sharply the filter transitions between pass and stop bands. A decibel (dB) scale is logarithmic rather than linear: a change in power by a factor of 10 corresponds to a 10 dB change in level. In practice, attenuation of around 40 dB below the original magnitude means that frequency component has been effectively removed.
Before choosing filter settings, it helps to examine the frequency composition of your raw signal using a Fast Fourier Transform (FFT). Plotting the FFT of a section of baseline data alongside a section of active data lets you see where the real signal energy lies and whether any obvious noise peaks are present. This inspection should inform your filter design rather than simply copying settings from the literature.


Filter Types: High Pass, Low Pass, and Band Pass
Three filter types are commonly used in EMG analysis:

A high pass filter removes low-frequency components while preserving high-frequency components. It is useful for eliminating motion artifact and DC offset (a zero-frequency baseline shift).
A low pass filter removes high-frequency content while preserving low-frequency content. It is used when creating a smooth activation envelope from rectified EMG.
A band pass filter applies both a high pass and a low pass cutoff simultaneously, preserving a specified frequency range and discarding frequencies both below and above it.

The terminology can be confusing at first. “High pass” means the filter passes high frequencies and blocks low ones. “Low pass” means the filter passes low frequencies and blocks high ones. A band pass filter is the combination.


Common Sources of EMG Noise and the Physiological Signal Range
Designing a good filter requires knowing something about both the noise you want to remove and the physiological signal you want to keep.
Common noise sources include:

Motion artifact — arises when wires or electrodes move during recording, acting as an antenna. This is more common with wired systems than wireless ones. Motion artifact typically appears at frequencies below approximately 20 Hz, with some literature citing up to 25 Hz (De Luca, Gilmore & Kuznetsov, 2010).
AC electrical line noise — appears at 60 Hz in the United States and at 50 Hz in countries using that electrical standard. A hardware notch filter is often used to attenuate this frequency before data are saved; you can detect its presence in your data by looking for a characteristic dip at 60 Hz in the FFT.
Radio frequency interference — can occur if a strong broadcast signal is present near the recording environment.
Ultrasound interference from sonomicrometry — when sonomicrometry and EMG are recorded simultaneously, the ultrasound pulses can be picked up by EMG electrodes. The interference frequency depends on the instrument’s pulse repetition rate and configuration; confirm the affected range from your system’s documentation and by inspecting the FFT of your own data.
Cardiac artifact — the heart’s electrical signal (ECG) can appear as noise in EMG recordings, particularly in recordings from muscles near the chest.

The physiologically relevant EMG frequency range: Motor unit action potentials span roughly 20 Hz to 450 Hz, and this range guides filter design. The lower boundary overlaps with some noise sources (motion artifact, 60 Hz line noise), which is why the exact filter settings matter and should be chosen thoughtfully rather than copied from the literature without inspection.


Filter Parameters: Cutoff Frequency and Filter Order
Two parameters define a digital filter:
Cutoff frequency marks the transition between the pass band and stop band. In practice, no filter has a perfectly vertical transition, so the stop band and pass band are specified as separate frequencies, and the cutoff falls between them in the roll-off region. In MATLAB, filter design functions work with frequencies normalized to the Nyquist frequency (= sampling frequency ÷ 2), which is the theoretical upper limit on analyzable signal content.
Filter order controls the sharpness of the roll-off. A higher order produces a steeper transition — more closely approximating an ideal square-wave filter — but introduces a real cost: high-order filters can introduce ringing artifacts into the filtered signal. For example, a signal that is entirely positive in the raw data may briefly dip below zero after filtering with a high-order filter. This is not a property of the data; it is an artifact of the filter design. The general recommendation is to use the lowest filter order that is adequate for your data, and to always compare the raw and filtered signals visually as a reality check.
MATLAB’s filtfilt function applies the filter forward and then backward through the data. This zero-phase approach prevents time shifts in the filtered signal, but it also doubles the effective filter order relative to the specified design order. If you specify a second-order Butterworth filter and apply it with filtfilt, the result has an effective order of four.


Practical EMG Filtering in MATLAB
The core MATLAB functions for Butterworth filter design and application are:

buttord — determines the minimum filter order and cutoff frequency needed to meet specified stop band and pass band performance criteria (including stop band attenuation and pass band ripple tolerances).
butter — computes the filter coefficients from the order and cutoff frequency.
filtfilt — applies the filter forward and backward for zero-phase filtering.

For a high pass filter, a single stop band frequency and pass band frequency are provided. For a band pass filter, vectors of two frequencies are provided for each; providing two values automatically configures MATLAB’s Butterworth functions for bandpass mode.
Example: high pass filter. With a stop band at 30 Hz (to remove motion artifact) and a pass band starting at 90 Hz (to additionally clear 60 Hz noise), with a 5,000 Hz sampling rate, buttord yields filter order 5 with a cutoff frequency of approximately 75 Hz. Because this example dataset had already been processed with a hardware notch filter at 60 Hz, the main effect of the high pass filter was removal of the DC offset.
Example: band pass filter. With stop bands at 30 Hz and 1,200 Hz and a pass band of 90–800 Hz, buttord yields filter order 9 with cutoffs at approximately 83 Hz and 855 Hz. A band pass filter is appropriate when noise at higher frequencies — for example, from a sonomicrometry system — needs to be removed in addition to low-frequency noise.
When evaluating filter settings, always plot filtered and raw signals together. Useful checks: Is the overall shape preserved? Does the filtered signal ever cross zero in regions where the raw signal clearly should not? Is there obvious attenuation of peaks that should represent real physiological activity? Adjust parameters and repeat the visual inspection rather than committing to settings without this step.
Hardware filtering provided by a data acquisition system (such as a bandpass hardware filter in a wireless EMG system) reduces the need for aggressive software filtering. When hardware has already attenuated most noise sources, a simpler software filter — for example, a second-order high pass filter at 25 Hz applied with filtfilt — may be fully adequate.


Creating a Smooth Linear Envelope
After applying the initial high pass or band pass filter to the raw EMG, the signal can be rectified (taking the absolute value of each sample) to convert it to a fully positive representation. The positive and negative deflections in raw EMG are not independently meaningful; rectification pools them.
A second, low pass filter applied to the rectified signal produces a smooth linear envelope — a curve that approximates the time course of muscle activation. A widely used approach is a 4th order low pass Butterworth filter with a 10 Hz cutoff (Winter, 2009); because filtfilt doubles the effective order, specifying 2nd order in MATLAB achieves this. The optimal cutoff depends on movement speed: slower movements (e.g., walking) may warrant a lower cutoff (3–6 Hz), while faster tasks may require a higher one (up to ~20 Hz).
The order of operations matters. The high pass or band pass filter must be applied to the raw (un-rectified) signal first. Applying a high pass filter to an already-rectified signal can introduce artifacts because the rectified signal is always positive, and the high pass filter may force portions of it below zero — introducing a feature that was not present in the original data.
A limitation of the smooth linear envelope approach is that applying a single low pass filter attenuates higher-frequency components of the signal more than lower-frequency ones. As a result, it better captures the activation timing of slow motor units and may miss fast bursts of activity. A wavelet-based alternative addresses this by using a bank of filters spanning the physiological action potential range (approximately 20–450 Hz). Each wavelet in the bank acts as a narrow band pass filter; summing magnitudes across all wavelets produces an envelope that captures activation at both slow and fast frequencies more evenly than a single low pass filter.


Surface EMG Considerations and Electrode Configuration
Surface EMG and indwelling (needle or wire) EMG differ in several practically relevant ways. Surface EMG is typically sampled at approximately 1,000 Hz, in line with SENIAM guidelines (Hermens et al., 2000), whereas indwelling recordings often use higher rates (e.g., 5,000 Hz) to capture a broader frequency range. Surface EMG is subject to crosstalk — signal from adjacent muscles contaminating the recording — and the signal characteristics vary with electrode placement relative to the motor end plate.
When frequency composition needs to be precisely characterized at the individual muscle level, indwelling electrodes provide cleaner isolation. For most surface EMG applications, anatomical knowledge and careful electrode placement are sufficient to minimize crosstalk.
High-density electrode arrays offer a middle ground: multiple electrodes placed in a grid allow spatial decomposition of EMG components, analogous to the spatial filtering used in EEG. Software provided with dedicated high-density EMG systems automates much of this decomposition.
When using FFT analysis to characterize noise and signal composition, a useful strategy is to compute the FFT on a segment of baseline (pre-task) data and on a segment containing the signal of interest, then compare the two spectra. This makes it easier to identify which frequency bands contain real signal versus noise, and to select filter settings accordingly.

title: Scaling and dimensional analysis
text:
Overview

Gait types and their mechanical signatures
Legged animals use only a small number of stereotyped movement patterns called gaits. For striding bipeds — including humans, ostriches, and most ground birds — the two primary gaits are walking and running. These gaits can be distinguished both by foot-contact timing and by the dynamics of the body’s center of mass.
Duty factor is the ratio of stance duration to stride duration and provides a concise gait descriptor. When duty factor exceeds 0.5, there is a period of double support in which both limbs contact the ground simultaneously; this is the hallmark of walking. When duty factor falls below 0.5, there is an aerial phase in which no limbs contact the ground; this characterizes running gaits. Some birds also use a grounded running gait, in which running-like spring dynamics occur at low duty factors that still retain brief periods of overlapping limb support — a gait not commonly observed in humans.
Walking — inverted pendulum dynamics. During walking, the body can be approximated as a point mass vaulting over a relatively stiff leg. As the leg contacts the ground, the body is moving fastest and at its lowest height; as it arcs over the stance leg to mid-stance, it rises to its greatest height and decelerates. Gravitational potential energy and kinetic energy therefore fluctuate out of phase, and this passive exchange reduces the external mechanical work required to move the center of mass. This inverted-pendulum mechanism makes the stance phase of walking mechanically economical.
Running — spring-mass dynamics. At higher speeds, the pattern reverses. The leg compresses like a spring during stance, so the body is at its lowest height at mid-stance rather than its highest. Kinetic energy and gravitational potential energy now fluctuate in phase — both decrease during the first half of stance and increase during the second half — making direct exchange between them impossible. Instead, energy is stored in and returned from elastic structures in the limb (tendons, ligaments, and musculotendinous units), analogous to a bouncing mass on a spring.


Physical models for walking and running
The mass-spring (or spring-mass) model represents the runner as a point mass supported by a single massless spring leg. Despite its simplicity, this model captures the ground-reaction-force magnitude and timing observed across a wide range of running animals and speeds.
A key limitation of the single-leg inverted-pendulum model of walking is that it predicts a smooth, single-humped vertical ground-reaction-force trace, whereas the measured force during human (and animal) walking has a characteristic double-humped, M-shaped profile. Geyer, Seyfarth, and Blickhan (2006) resolved this by extending the spring-mass model to two legs. Their two-legged spring model reproduces the M-shaped ground-reaction-force profile and demonstrates that walking gaits can be viewed as a spring-loaded inverted pendulum (SLIP), with the same basic leg-spring mechanics underlying both walking and running. The SLIP model has since become the standard template model for studying gait dynamics across species.


Geometric similarity and the scaling challenge
A foundational concept for comparing animals of different sizes is isometric scaling (also called geometric similarity): what happens to lengths, areas, and volumes when an animal is simply scaled up in size without changing shape?
If linear dimensions (such as leg length, L) scale up by some factor, then:

Cross-sectional area scales as L²
Volume (and, assuming constant tissue density, body mass) scales as L³

This creates a fundamental mechanical challenge with increasing body size. Muscular and skeletal strength is proportional to the cross-sectional area of tissues, which scales as L². Body weight, which must be supported and accelerated, scales as L³. The ratio of strength to body weight therefore scales as 1/L: larger animals are relatively weaker under isometric scaling. To compensate, larger animals tend to adopt a more upright, straighter-legged posture, which orients the skeleton more vertically and reduces the muscular force required to support body weight in stance.


The dynamic similarity hypothesis
Geometric similarity describes shape; it does not predict whether animals of different sizes move in functionally similar ways. To address locomotor function across size, Alexander and Jayes (1983) developed the dynamic similarity hypothesis: animals of different sizes move in dynamically similar ways — using mechanically equivalent gaits — if their dimensionless gait parameters are equivalent when normalized by an appropriate set of characteristic physical quantities.
This is both a theoretical prediction and an empirical hypothesis that can be tested with data. If locomotor function scales in a dynamically similar manner, size-related differences in absolute gait measures (stride frequency, stride length, speed) should disappear once the data are expressed as dimensionless quantities. Deviations from collapse reveal genuine functional differences across size.


Dimensionless quantities for locomotion analysis
The appropriate set of normalizing quantities for legged terrestrial locomotion can be derived from the physics of the spring-loaded inverted pendulum. The key physical parameters governing these dynamics are body mass (M), leg length (L), and gravitational acceleration (g). Using these as base quantities, dimensionless forms of all gait variables can be derived:



Quantity
Dimensionless form




Length / distance
Divide by L


Force
Divide by Mg


Time
Divide by \(\sqrt{L/g}\) (pendular period)


Frequency
Multiply by \(\sqrt{L/g}\)


Speed
Divide by \(\sqrt{gL}\)


Energy / work
Divide by MgL



McMahon and Cheng (1990) applied this normalizing framework to the spring-mass running model, formalizing dimensionless parameters for running mechanics that include dimensionless leg stiffness and dimensionless peak force in addition to dimensionless speed.
Froude number. A particularly important dimensionless quantity is the Froude number, defined as:
\[Fr = \frac{V^2}{gL}\]
The Froude number is the ratio of inertial (kinetic) energy to gravitational (potential) energy in the system, and its square root equals the dimensionless speed. The Froude number has a physical significance for walking: as a legged system using inverted-pendulum mechanics increases speed, the centripetal acceleration required to maintain contact with the ground during the arc of stance increases. When Fr = 1, this centripetal acceleration equals gravitational acceleration, and the system is on the verge of becoming airborne at mid-stance. Walking with purely inverted-pendulum dynamics is therefore physically impossible above Fr = 1; an aerial phase naturally emerges. Measured walk-to-run transitions in many animals occur near this theoretical limit, supporting the utility of the Froude number as a dimensionless speed benchmark.
Note that the dimensionless speed (V / \(\sqrt{gL}\)) equals the square root of the Froude number, so these two quantities are related but differ at values away from 1; some sources use one, some the other.


Scaling patterns in avian bipedal locomotion
Ground birds offer an excellent comparative system for testing dynamic similarity in locomotion. A compiled dataset spanning a 2,500-fold range in body mass — from painted quail to ostriches, drawing on 21 species from the literature — provides a rigorous test of whether dimensionless normalization collapses cross-species variation in gait (Daley & Birn-Jeffery 2018).
In absolute (SI) units, large birds operate at much lower stride frequencies and take longer strides than small birds, and maximum absolute speed increases with body size. These differences are expected simply from size.
After normalization to dimensionless quantities, two key patterns emerge:

The large variation in stride frequency across species compresses substantially, but the rank order inverts: large birds (ostriches) use relatively higher dimensionless stride frequencies than small birds (quail), the opposite of the absolute pattern.
Large birds use relatively shorter dimensionless stride lengths than small birds.

These patterns are consistent with differences in center-of-mass trajectory between size classes. Large birds tend to use a more vertically bouncy running gait, with greater vertical oscillation of the center of mass. Small birds tend to use a flatter center-of-mass trajectory with longer relative strides. The vertically bouncy gait of large birds is associated with reduced fore-aft ground-reaction-force fluctuations, which reduces the mechanical work demand per stride — a potential functional advantage at large body size.
Ostriches are notable outliers even within the large-bird category: they use exceptionally high relative stride frequencies, which has been interpreted as reflecting well-developed elastic energy storage and return mechanisms in the distal limb (tendons and ligaments) that may also assist in accelerating the leg during swing via elastic catapult mechanisms.


Practical considerations for cross-species and cross-population comparisons
Several analytical choices affect the validity of dimensionless normalization and should be made deliberately based on the task at hand.
Defining leg length. Standing hip height is the most commonly used measure of leg length in comparative locomotion studies, because it approximates the resting leg length and is straightforward to measure consistently across species. However, hip height conflates body size with posture: larger animals adopt more upright postures, so hip height grows faster than skeletal segment length with increasing body mass. Alternative approaches include using the sum of limb-segment lengths (which reflects maximum extension capacity and may be more appropriate for jumping analyses) or limb-segment lengths back-calculated assuming isometric scaling. The appropriate choice depends on which aspect of the mechanical task is most relevant.
Including or excluding the foot. Whether the foot should be included in leg length depends on how the animal contacts the ground during the task of interest. Plantigrade animals (full foot contact) have an effective leg length from hip to ankle during walking, but digitigrade or unguligrade animals contact the ground on their toes or hooves, functionally incorporating the foot or metatarsus into the leg. For activities like running where contact point and posture vary, measuring the hip-to-center-of-pressure distance during the actual task provides the most functionally relevant leg length.
Applying to individuals with atypical anatomy. The same first-principles reasoning applies when scaling analyses are extended to individuals whose anatomy differs from population norms — for example, in the context of para-athletes or individuals with limb differences. The key quantity to identify is the effective leg length for the specific task: the distance from the body’s center of mass to the point of ground contact, whatever the anatomy in between. Identifying this effective length, and understanding the physics of the task it governs, provides the foundation for meaningful comparison.
Measuring comparable speed ranges. Comparing maximum speed across species is methodologically difficult: the speed range an animal will use in a laboratory differs from what it achieves in overground conditions, and the conditions required to elicit true maximum effort differ by species. These sampling differences should be considered carefully when interpreting cross-species comparisons, particularly at the extremes of the speed distribution.

title: Cross-bridge kinetics & experimental system analysis methods
text:
Overview

Experimental preparations
The experiments described in this workshop use demembranated (chemically skinned) muscle fibers, in which the cell membrane has been removed. Without an intact membrane, the intracellular environment is controlled entirely by the bathing solution — calcium concentration, ATP level, and ionic strength can all be set independently. This differs fundamentally from electrically stimulated whole-muscle or intact-fiber preparations.
For cardiac studies, the preparation is a multicellular myocardial strip dissected from the ventricular wall or papillary muscle and trimmed to a small piece of tissue. Published cardiac strip preparations span a wide range of dimensions (roughly 100–500 µm wide and 400–1200 µm long), with specific values depending on laboratory protocol and tissue source. For single skeletal muscle fiber experiments, fibers are trimmed to approximately 2–3 mm in length; fiber diameter typically falls in the range of 50–120 µm, varying by fiber type and species. One end of each preparation is attached to a force transducer and the other to a length-controlling motor. Sarcomere length can be set directly by imaging the regular thick-and-thin-filament striations visible under light microscopy.


The cross-bridge cycle
Force production in striated muscle is driven by the cyclic interaction of myosin (thick-filament motor) with actin (thin filament). Thin filament activation begins when calcium binds to troponin C (TnC); this propagates through the troponin complex (TnI and TnT), shifting tropomyosin from the blocked to the open state and exposing myosin-binding sites on actin (McKillop & Geeves, 1993).
Myosin binds to actin in a post-hydrolysis state bearing both ADP and inorganic phosphate (Pi) — the M·ADP·Pi state first characterized by Lymn and Taylor (1971). In the widely accepted mechanochemical model, Pi release from the catalytic site is associated with the force-generating conformational change (the power stroke, or lever-arm rotation), producing the strongly-bound, force-bearing cross-bridge. It is important to note, however, that the exact mechanistic ordering of lever-arm rotation and Pi exit remains an area of active investigation. Single-molecule studies have raised the possibility that an initial lever-arm movement precedes Pi departure, with Pi release then stabilizing the post-stroke configuration (Dantzig et al., 1992; Woody et al., 2019). Pi release is therefore best described as functionally coupled to force generation, even if the mechanistic sequence is not fully resolved.
Following Pi release, ADP dissociates from the AM·ADP complex. ADP release is rate-limiting specifically for the detachment transition — it governs how long the cross-bridge remains in the strongly-bound state before ATP can bind. This role is well established at physiological ATP concentrations (Siemankowski et al., 1985; Geeves & Holmes, 1999). Importantly, ADP release is strain-dependent: under mechanical load, ADP release is further slowed, and this is one mechanism by which applied force modulates the cross-bridge cycling rate (Nyitrai & Geeves, 2004). Finally, ATP binding to the rigor AM complex causes rapid myosin detachment from actin. The freed M·ATP complex then hydrolyzes ATP to M·ADP·Pi, restoring the high-actin-affinity pre-stroke state and enabling the next cycle.


Passive mechanics and the force-length relationship
Striated muscle produces both passive (resting) and active (calcium-activated) force. Passive tension arises from intracellular and extracellular structural proteins. Titin — a giant elastic protein spanning from the Z-disk to the M-line of each sarcomere — is the dominant intracellular spring element, particularly at moderate sarcomere lengths. Collagen in the extracellular matrix (perimysium and endomysium) is the major extracellular contributor and becomes increasingly important at longer lengths (Granzier & Irving, 1995; Wang et al., 1991).
The active force-length relationship follows the classic Gordon-Huxley-Julian description (Gordon et al., 1966): as sarcomere length increases from short lengths, active force rises along an ascending limb as thick-thin filament overlap grows; it plateaus at optimal overlap; and then declines along a descending limb as overlap is lost at very long lengths. Total force at any given length is the sum of passive and active contributions.


Length-dependent activation and the Frank-Starling mechanism
At the organ level, the Frank-Starling law describes the increase in cardiac stroke volume that accompanies greater ventricular filling. At the cellular and molecular level, the analog is length-dependent activation: increasing sarcomere length within the physiological range augments both peak active force and calcium sensitivity (a leftward shift of the force-pCa curve), independent of changes in filament overlap (Kentish et al., 1986; Allen & Kentish, 1985). This is the established cellular basis of the Frank-Starling mechanism.
Cross-bridge kinetics may also contribute to this length dependence. In rat myocardial strips studied by sinusoidal perturbation analysis, cross-bridge attachment time increases and cycling rate slows as sarcomere length increases. The mechanistic interpretation is that ADP release — the rate-limiting step for the detachment transition — is sensitive to the mechanical strain on the cross-bridge: at longer sarcomere lengths and higher internal forces, the geometry of the catalytic pocket may slow ADP exit, prolonging attachment and increasing force per cross-bridge. This finding is qualitative; the specific quantitative kinetic parameters at each sarcomere length require confirmation and citation from the primary data publication from the Tanner lab.
Conversely, at shorter sarcomere lengths, faster cross-bridge detachment may facilitate relaxation. Together, these sarcomere length-dependent changes in ADP release rate represent a kinetic contribution to the Frank-Starling mechanism that operates alongside, and may amplify, the contributions from calcium sensitivity and filament overlap.


Myosin isoforms and cross-bridge kinetic sensitivity
The magnitude of length-dependent kinetic sensitivity varies markedly with myosin isoform. In mice and rats, the predominant cardiac myosin isoform is alpha-myosin heavy chain (alpha-MHC, MYH6), which has a high actin-activated ATPase rate and fast shortening velocity (Lompre et al., 1979). In larger animals — guinea pigs and above — beta-myosin heavy chain (beta-MHC, MYH7) predominates; this slower, higher-economy isoform is also the primary human ventricular myosin. Rabbits represent an intermediate case: their ventricles are predominantly beta-MHC but retain a variable alpha-MHC component depending on age and hormonal status.
In skeletal muscle, slow-twitch (type I / beta-MHC) fibers show greater length-dependent sensitivity than fast-twitch (type II / alpha-MHC) fibers. This is most clearly documented for calcium sensitivity of force; the extent to which cross-bridge kinetics specifically (as opposed to steady-state force and calcium sensitivity) are more length-sensitive in slow-twitch fibers is supported by experimental evidence but is less comprehensively characterized. Fast-twitch myosin kinetics appear comparatively insensitive to changes in sarcomere length.


System analysis: sinusoidal perturbation, step-stretch, and the ABC model
Sinusoidal analysis. In sinusoidal length perturbation analysis, the muscle length is oscillated at a series of frequencies while force is recorded. Muscle behaves as a linear viscoelastic system: the force output is also sinusoidal but phase-shifted relative to the length input. The in-phase component defines the elastic modulus (reflecting cross-bridge attachment stiffness); the out-of-phase component defines the viscous modulus (reflecting energy dissipation and cross-bridge cycling dynamics). Mapping how these two moduli change across frequency resolves kinetic processes operating at different time scales. In practice, stochastic (white-noise) length perturbations — a sum of many sine waves applied simultaneously — can be used instead of single-frequency sweeps; the underlying mathematics and the moduli extracted are equivalent, but the raw data appearance differs.
A frequency sweep requires the preparation to remain maximally activated throughout. For slow myosin isoforms or low-temperature experiments where the lowest probe frequencies must be in the 0.1–1 Hz range, a complete sweep can take approximately one to two minutes — long enough for measurable tissue deterioration. This constrains how many sweeps can be obtained from a single preparation.
Step-stretch analysis. A step-stretch protocol applies a rapid length step (completed in milliseconds) and records the transient force response, which can be analyzed in a few seconds of record. This dramatically reduces activation time per measurement. In active muscle, a step stretch produces a stereotyped multi-phase transient: Phase 1 is the rapid elastic force rise as cross-bridges are stretched (to T1); Phase 2 is fast tension decay as stretched cross-bridges detach (from T1 toward T2); Phase 3 is a slower tension recovery as new cross-bridges recruit (from T2 toward T3). The T1/T2 tension-transient framework and the mechanistic interpretation of these phases were established by Huxley AF and Simmons RM (1971). The fuller characterization of the Phase 3 recovery — driven by cross-bridge recruitment — was elaborated in the companion study by Ford LE, Huxley AF, and Simmons RM (1977):

Huxley AF, Simmons RM (1971). Proposed mechanism of force generation in striated muscle. Nature 233: 533–538. DOI: 10.1038/233533a0.


Ford LE, Huxley AF, Simmons RM (1977). Tension responses to sudden length change in stimulated frog muscle fibres near slack length. J Physiol 269: 441–515.

Fast-twitch fibers complete their step-stretch transient in ~250 ms; slow-twitch fibers (e.g., soleus) require up to a full second, reflecting slower cross-bridge cycling. These different time scales affect which fitting approaches work best: a dual-exponential function with offset may fit slow-twitch transients cleanly, while fast-twitch transients — where all three phases overlap in time — require more complex methods (e.g., the ABC model in the time domain).
The ABC process model. Frequency-domain data from sinusoidal analysis are typically fit to a three-component model introduced by Kawai M and Brandt PW (1980):

Kawai M, Brandt PW (1980). Sinusoidal analysis: a high resolution method for correlating biochemical reactions with physiological processes in activated skeletal muscles of rabbit, frog and crayfish. J Muscle Res Cell Motil 1(3): 279–303.

The three processes, ordered by ascending characteristic frequency, are:

Process A (slowest, rate 2πA): associated with slow regulatory dynamics — including thin filament cooperativity and tropomyosin kinetics — as well as passive viscoelastic elements. Labeling it purely “passive” oversimplifies its biological content, particularly in sub-maximally activated preparations.
Process B (intermediate, rate 2πB): associated with cross-bridge recruitment — the apparent rate at which myosin attaches to actin.
Process C (fastest, rate 2πC): associated with the force-generating kinetic step, most often interpreted in terms of the Pi-release / power-stroke transition rate. Its inverse is used as an approximation of cross-bridge attachment time, though it more precisely reflects the forward and reverse rates of the force-generating step rather than the myosin off-rate from actin directly (Kawai & Halvorson, 1991).

This approach was adapted from frequency-domain methods developed earlier for insect asynchronous flight muscle. John Pringle (Oxford) pioneered frequency-dependent mechanical characterization of insect fibrillar muscle from the 1950s onward (Pringle, 1954; Pringle, 1967; Pringle, 1978), establishing the conceptual and analytical foundation before Kawai and Brandt applied sinusoidal analysis to vertebrate preparations.
Data fitting tools. MATLAB scripts developed in the Tanner lab (with contributions from Maddy Chastain) implement fitting routines for both sinusoidal and step-stretch data. These scripts extract the ABC process parameters from sinusoidal sweeps and estimate ADP release and ATP binding rates from step-stretch data obtained at varying ATP concentrations. Separate script versions are provided for Windows and macOS (the MATLAB crosshair function used for interactive point selection in some routines is not available on macOS). Data sets include human cardiac sinusoidal data, human cardiac step-stretch data, and rat skeletal muscle step-stretch data from fast-twitch (medial gastrocnemius) and slow-twitch (soleus) fibers.
